papers.title: Five-Year Changes in Nurses' Compassion Competence and Associated Factors: A Longitudinal Study Using Explainable Machine Learning.
papers.abstract: To examine 5-year changes in nurses' compassion competence and identify personal and job-related factors associated with these changes within the Job Demands-Resources framework. Compassion competence is a dynamic professional competency shaped by individual capacities and work environments, but its long-term change has rarely been examined. In this secondary analysis of a national Korean cohort, 332 hospital nurses who responded in 2018 (T1) and 2022 (T5) with complete data were analyzed using paired t-tests, simultaneous multiple linear regression, and linear mixed-effects growth models. Random Forest, eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) models were evaluated using 100 repetitions of 5-fold cross-validation, and feature importance was quantified using mean absolute SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) values. Compassion competence increased from T1 to T5 (mean change = 0.09, p < 0.001; 0.023 points per year in the growth model). The regression model explained 10.3% of the variance, and only baseline age was significantly (negatively) associated with change. The ensemble models showed higher in-sample fit (R2 = 0.33-0.41) but negative mean cross-validated R2 values. Changes in nurse participation in hospital affairs (positive direction) and in staffing and resource adequacy (negative direction) were the most important features in all ensemble models, with rankings and directions that were stable across folds, although their regression coefficients were not statistically significant. Nurses' compassion competence increased modestly over 5 years, supporting its conceptualization as a dynamic professional competency. Nursing work environment features were the most prominent, but exploratory, model-based contributors. Nurse managers may consider nurses' participation in hospital affairs and staffing when supporting compassionate practice; however, these factors should be evaluated in intervention studies before being adopted as management targets.

papers.title: A Bayesian functional model with multilevel partition priors for group studies in neuroscience.
papers.abstract: The statistical analysis of group studies in neuroscience is particularly challenging due to the complex spatio-temporal nature of the data, its multiple levels and the inter-individual variability in brain responses. Traditional ANOVA-based studies and linear mixed effects models typically provide only a limited exploration of the dynamics of group brain activity and of the variability in individual responses, potentially leading to overly simplistic conclusions and/or missing more intricate patterns. In this study we propose a novel Bayesian model-based clustering approach for functional data that simultaneously assesses group effects and individual deviations across the main temporal features in the data. To this end, we develop a multilevel partition prior to model the functional scores arising from a functional Principal Components decomposition of neuroscientific recordings. The proposed approach enables a thorough exploration of group differences and individual deviations without compromising on the spatio-temporal nature of the data. Through a simulation study we demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves correct classification in different clustering scenarios under low and high noise levels in the data. Finally, we consider an Electroencephalogram case study involving an object recognition task, where the proposed approach provides new insights into the underlying brain mechanisms generating the data and their variability.

papers.title: Finding rhythm: Individualizing the timing of home nutrition support.
papers.abstract: While overnight cyclic infusions are considered standard clinical practice for home nutrition support therapy, particularly for parenteral nutrition, there is growing recognition that the optimal timing of infusion may vary among patients. A key clinical dilemma is determining the optimal timing of infusion schedules, which vary based on modality, tolerance, metabolic needs, and patient preference. Guidance from the American Society for Parenteral and Enteral Nutrition (ASPEN) and the European Society for Clinical Nutrition and Metabolism (ESPEN) offers flexibility in selecting between daytime and nighttime infusion schedules. Overnight infusions largely reflect hospital-based cyclic regimens and offer advantages such as improved daytime independence and mobility, discretion, and potentially enhanced adherence and better tolerance with longer infusion cycles. However, advances in portable technology and a growing understanding of the role of the circadian system in governing metabolism, appetite, immune and inflammatory function, and aging have increased consideration of daytime infusions, which may better align with circadian rhythms and improve sleep quality by reducing nighttime disruptions. Selecting an optimal infusion schedule requires a patient-centered approach that balances clinical goals with quality of life, psychosocial factors, sleep, daily routines, and safety. Infusion schedule changes should be carefully monitored for tolerance, nutrition adequacy, and safety. Infusion timing should be tailored through ongoing collaboration between patients and interdisciplinary teams, with regular reassessment to ensure safety, effectiveness, and alignment with evolving patient needs.
papers.journal: Nutrition in clinical practice : official publication of the American Society for Parenteral and Enteral Nutrition

papers.title: Creatine supplementation effects on cognition, sleep, and menopause symptoms in response to six weeks of high-intensity resistance training in perimenopausal females.
papers.abstract: Perimenopause (PERI) women experience cognitive dysfunction, sleep disturbances, and menopause-related symptoms, yet few accessible and time-efficient interventions have been evaluated. The purpose of the current study was to determine the impact of creatine monohydrate (CM) during six weeks of high-intensity resistance training (HIRT) on cognition, sleep, and menopause symptoms in PERI females. PERI females (n = 51; Age: 46 ± 5 yrs) were randomized to CM (n = 18), placebo (PLA) (n = 20), or a non-training control (CON) group (n = 13). CM and PLA groups completed a 5-day loading phase (20 g·day⁻¹) followed by six weeks of maintenance (~ 4.5 g·day⁻¹) combined with twice-weekly progressive HIRT. Cognitive performance (Stroop, Rey 15-item memory test) and prefrontal oxygenation via functional near-infrared spectroscopy were assessed at baseline (BASE), pre- (PRE), and post-training (POST). Sleep and self-reported menopause symptoms (temperature sensitivity, fatigue, soreness, brain fog, and bloating) were monitored daily using a WHOOP wearable wristband. Stroop reaction time improved over time (congruent: p < 0.001; incongruent: p = 0.004) with no group differences. Prefrontal oxygenation during the Stroop test increased with CM at POST (+ 0.32 ± 2.01%) compared to a decrease with PLA (- 1.62 ± 2.01%; p = 0.003). Sleep consistency showed a time × treatment interaction (p < 0.001), with higher consistency in CM than PLA at week 6 (baseline-adjusted mean difference: +7.4% points, p = 0.015). In this exploratory analysis, CM combined with HIRT was associated with greater prefrontal oxygenation, higher sleep consistency, and fewer self-reported temperature sensitivity days relative to PLA in PERI females.

papers.title: Conceptual Frameworks and Assessment of Readiness to Train in Endurance Exercise: A Systematic Review.
papers.abstract: Readiness to train has emerged as a construct to guide daily training prescription and recovery management in endurance athletes. However, its conceptual basis, assessment, and methodological quality and validity remain inconsistently defined. This systematic review aimed to (1) identify how readiness is defined in endurance exercise and (2) categorize tools used to assess it. As a secondary aim, the review evaluated the methodological approach of the studies employing these tools. Following PRISMA guidelines, PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were explored. Eligible studies included endurance athletes aged 18-65 years, evaluating readiness before or after training or competition. Two reviewers independently screened, extracted data, and assessed quality using the revised Cochrane Risk of Bias tool. Fourteen studies were included. Readiness definitions were inconsistent and frequently overlapped with related constructs such as recovery and fatigue. Ten studies used self-reported tools (fatigue, sleep, stress, and soreness). Nine studies assessed objective tools, including heart rate (HR) variability, resting HR, countermovement jump, and submaximal tests. HR variability-based approaches and individualized feedback were used to track autonomic recovery and guide training prescription, while on-field indices (eg, HR-running speed, HR-running power, countermovement jump) provided neuromuscular insights, although they can also be influenced by cardiovascular and metabolic factors. Overall, there was considerable heterogeneity in tools and their combinations, highlighting the lack of standardized approaches to assess readiness to train. Seven studies combined subjective and objective measures, suggesting a more comprehensive monitoring strategy. However, many of these tools were primarily used to assess related constructs (eg, fatigue, recovery, and training adaptation) rather than directly predict performance; consequently, their ability to predict performance outcomes remained limited or was not even assessed. This review highlights substantial conceptual ambiguity, methodological limitations, and heterogeneity in readiness assessment. A multidimensional framework conceptualizing readiness as a dynamic psychophysiological state influenced by stress, recovery, and contextual factors may support more structured and meaningful monitoring in endurance athletes.

papers.title: 24-Hour Movement Guideline Compliance and Physical Fitness in Uruguayan Preschoolers: The Role of Specific Behavior Combinations.
papers.abstract: The 24-hour movement paradigm emphasizes the interdependence of total physical activity, sleep, and screen time (ST). This study analyzed adherence to World Health Organization guidelines and the association of specific compliance combinations with physical fitness in preschoolers from Rivera, Uruguay. Data from the pilot phase of the SUNRISE study in Uruguay were used. Total physical activity and sleep were measured via accelerometry; ST was parent-reported. A Composite Physical Fitness Z-Score was derived from 6 tests (PREFIT/SUNRISE). Linear regression models assessed associations between behaviors and fitness, adjusting for sex, age, and socioeconomic status. The sample comprised 135 children (mean age 3.8 [0.5] y; 50.4% boys). Only 11.9% met all guidelines; 20.0% met none. A higher Total Compliance Score (representing the total number of guidelines met, ranging from 0 to 3) was linearly associated with better fitness (β = 0.106; 95% CI, 0.012 to 0.200). Regarding specific compliance combinations, meeting total physical activity + ST guidelines showed a strong association with fitness (β = 0.507; 95% CI, 0.054 to 0.959), exhibiting a stronger association than meeting all 3 guidelines, which was only marginally significant. Compliance with the ST guideline was the only individual predictor independently associated with fitness. Guideline compliance is low in this population. High physical activity combined with limited ST was strongly associated with optimal physical fitness, suggesting that the "move more, sit less" synergy is highly relevant for motor competence, independent of sleep duration. Consequently, interventions should prioritize protecting active play from digital displacement.

papers.title: A behavioral and electrophysiological study on the influence of menstrual cycle, estradiol and progesterone on the social approach-avoidance behavior tendencies of women.
papers.abstract: It remains unclear whether women's social approach-avoidance behaviors toward different facial expressions are influenced by their menstrual cycles, estradiol and progesterone levels, or what the underlying electrophysiological mechanisms might be. This study collected data on the levels of estradiol and progesterone, social approach-avoidance behavior and electroencephalogram (EEG) recordings from 27 women with natural menstrual cycles during three phases- early follicular phase, late follicular phase, and mid-luteal phase. The results showed that women in the late follicular phase exhibited a faster approach tendency and a smaller LPP amplitude to happy faces compared to the early follicular phase; women in the mid-luteal phase exhibited a faster approach tendency and a smaller LPP amplitude to fearful faces compared to the late follicular phase. Estradiol levels is positively correlated with the efficiency of approach behavior toward happy faces, while progesterone levels is positively correlated with the efficiency of approach behavior toward fearful faces. The results show that women's social approach-avoidance behaviors are specifically regulated by the menstrual cycle, estradiol and progesterone, and exhibit higher cognitive processing efficiency in the late positive potential (LPP) of the brain. These findings are manifestations in social interactions of the characteristics of women's interest pursuit and self-restraint under the influence of different sex hormones formed during evolution, updating established hormone-behavior links in social emotional contexts.

papers.title: The development of cool and hot inhibitory control from late childhood to young adulthood: An ERP study.
papers.abstract: Inhibitory control (IC) is not a unitary construct but involves cool and hot dimensions. Although their behavioral development is documented, little is known about their underlying neural dynamics from late childhood to early adulthood, with EEG evidence remaining scarce. Therefore, this study characterized the developmental trajectories of cool and hot IC and identified their associated electrophysiological patterns. Children, adolescents, and young adults completed two Stroop-like tasks: a cool Stroop task requiring color naming independent of word meaning, and a hot Stroop task requiring identification of facial emotional expressions independent of emotion words. Behavioral performances were assessed through reaction times and accuracy. ERP analyses focused on the N2, P3, and early and late stages of the Late Positive Potential (LPP). We showed that emotional context modulates behavioral performance, along with electrophysiological data revealing enhanced allocation of attentional resources to emotional information at early N2 and P3 stages and at the LPP stage, with stronger N2 and LPP effects in younger participants. ERP findings indicate that interference effects are reflected in late-stage processing as indexed by the LPP component, consistent with post-evaluative rather than early conflict-monitoring processes. Finally, although faces expressing low-intensity emotions might facilitate processing, this effect varies across development; by contrast, emotional conflict in adolescence increases late-stage processing demands, as indexed by late LPP modulation. This pattern is associated with a delayed maturation of hot IC compared to cool IC. Overall, these findings highlight the joint influence of emotion perception and development on conflict processing at behavioral and neural levels.

papers.title: Climate-induced extreme heat associated with suicide risk mediated by poor sleep and emotional dysregulation: A nationally representative panel study from Bangladesh.
papers.abstract: Climate change-induced heat exposure is an emerging public health concern with potential mental health consequences, including suicide risk. Yet, in climate-vulnerable low- and middle-income countries the association between heat exposure and suicide risk, and the mediating mechanisms underlying this connection, remain underexplored. Using a nationally representative two-round panel survey from Bangladesh (n=7,492), we empirically examined whether poor sleep quality and emotional dysregulation mediate the relationship between exposure to extreme heat and suicide risk. Risk was assessed using a validated suicide cognitions scale across two seasonal rounds surveying the same individuals. Exposure to days ≥28°C over a two-week period was the lowest temperature threshold significantly associated with elevated suicide risk, with the highest risk detected at ≥35°C. At this 35°C threshold, 29.5% of the total association was mediated through poor sleep quality and 1.8% through emotional dysregulation. Risk was notably higher during the summer, and among less educated and poorer populations. This study provides novel evidence from a climate-vulnerable country on psychosocial mechanisms connecting heat and suicidality. As heat extremes intensify across the Global South, targeted mental health interventions, both infrastructural and psychological, may need consideration in climate adaptation strategies to protect the well-being of at-risk populations.

papers.title: Multimodal evidence associated with 20Hz rTMS in AD: neuroaxonal injury reduction, neural oscillatory rebalancing, and multilayer network integration.
papers.abstract: High-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) has been demonstrated to enhance cognitive function in patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD), but the neurobiological mechanisms associated with neuroaxonal injury, neural oscillatory dynamics, and large-scale network reorganization remain unclear. In this study, we first conducted a randomized, sham-controlled trial with 16 patients with AD to evaluate the efficacy of DLPFC-targeted rTMS, followed by a single-arm multimodal cohort study of 30 patients to explore potential neurobiological mechanisms through cognitive assessments, blood biomarkers, EEG oscillatory activity, and multiplex brain network analysis. In Stage 1, the sham group showed no significant pre-post changes in MMSE or MoCA scores (MMSE: Z = -0.738, Cohen's r = 0.26; MoCA: Z =-0.853, Cohen's r = 0.30). The active rTMS group showed improvements in MMSE (Z = -2.124, Cohen's r = 0.75) and MoCA (Z = -2.108, Cohen's r = 0.75). In stage 2, rTMS was associated with improvements in MMSE (Z = -2.863, Cohen's r = 0.523) and MoCA (t = -6.137, Cohen's r = 0.752) scores. Biomarker analyses indicated a significant decrease in NfL concentrations (Z=-2.371, Cohen's r=0.484). EEG recordings revealed a decrease in delta power in the left temporal lobe (t=2.158, Cohen's r=0.372) and increases in beta power in the right parietal lobe and gamma power in the temporal lobe (beta: Z=-2.088, Cohen's r=0.381; gamma: Z=-2.129, Cohen's r=0.389). Network analysis showed reduced modularity and enhanced global efficiency across theta, alpha, and beta bands, accompanied by increased degree of overlap in frontal, parietal, and occipital regions. Importantly, MoCA improvement correlated with gamma-band global efficiency (R=0.389, P=0.034) and multilayer clustering coefficients in the left frontal and right occipital regions (R=0.478, P=0.008; R=0.398, P=0.029). Overall, rTMS exposure was associated with cognitive improvements in patients with AD, together with changes in neurodegeneration-related biomarkers and EEG network organization. These findings suggest that cognitive changes following rTMS may be associated with oscillatory modulation and large-scale network remodeling. papers.title: Implementation and early experience with tubular retractor-assisted minimally invasive parafascicular surgery for deep brain tumors.
papers.abstract: Minimally invasive parafascicular surgery using tubular retractors (tr-MIPS) has emerged as a strategy to access deep intra-axial lesions while minimizing white matter disruption. However, practical guidance on institutional implementation and integration with modern intraoperative adjuncts remains limited. We describe our early institutional experience with tr-MIPS, with a focus on workflow adoption, multimodal adjunct integration, and feasibility. Demographic, radiographic, operative, and postoperative data were collected, with particular attention to extent of resection, neurological outcomes, and use of adjunctive technologies. Six patients underwent tr-MIPS for deep intra-axial tumors of varied histology. Gross or near-total resection was achieved in four cases. Five patients experienced no new postoperative neurological deficits, and one had transient dysphasia. Median length of stay was 3.5 days. A range of adjuncts including diffusion tensor imaging, 5-aminolevulinic acid fluorescence, intraoperative neurophysiologic monitoring, and depth-electrode electroencephalography were successfully incorporated without workflow disruption. Notably, intraoperative depth-electrode EEG was used to guide resection of an epileptogenic lesion, representing a novel adjunctive application in the tr-MIPS setting. tr-MIPS can be implemented within a modern neurosurgical practice and feasibly integrated with multiple intraoperative adjuncts. We demonstrate feasibility with the addition of this technique to our center's armamentarium. Beyond facilitating access to deep lesions, its compatibility with technologies such as tractography, neurophysiologic monitoring, and EEG expands its functional utility. These findings support the feasibility of a broader adoption of tr-MIPS and highlight opportunities for multimodal, precision-guided minimally invasive neuro-oncologic surgery.

papers.title: Effect of circadian-oriented goal-directed sedation on sleep quality and clinical outcomes in mechanically ventilated ICU patients.
papers.abstract: Sleep disruption and circadian rhythm disturbances are common in mechanically ventilated intensive care unit (ICU) patients and are associated with delirium, prolonged ventilation, and poor clinical outcomes. Conventional sedation strategies may further impair sleep architecture and circadian regulation. Therefore, this study aimed to evaluate the effects of circadian-oriented, goal-directed sedation on sleep quality and clinical outcomes in mechanically ventilated ICU patients. This study enrolled 65 mechanically ventilated patients admitted to ICU at Suzhou Ninth People's Hospital between March 2024 and December 2024. Using convenience sampling, 33 patients admitted between March and July 2024 were allocated to the control group and received routine sedation and nursing care, while 32 patients admitted between August and December 2024 were formed the intervention group and received sedation management individualized according to circadian sleep-wake patterns. Sleep quality was assessed on days 1, 3, 5, and 7 after intervention using the Richards-Campbell Sleep Questionnaire (RCSQ) and a portable sleep monitor. Delirium was evaluated by Confusion Assessment Method for the ICU (CAM-ICU). Sedative dosage, duration of mechanical ventilation, length of ICU and hospital stay, , clinical improvement rate, complications, and hospitalization costs were compared between groups. Baseline characteristics were comparable between the two groups. Sleep quality improved over time in both groups; however, Richards-Campbell Sleep Questionnaire scores were significantly higher in the intervention group at all assessment points (p < 0.05). Patients receiving circadian-oriented sedation experienced shorter durations of mechanical ventilation, reduced ICU and total hospital stays, higher rates of clinical improvement, and lower hospitalization costs compared with the control group (p < 0.05). The incidence of complications, including delirium, was also significantly lower in the intervention group. Sedation management aligned with circadian sleep-wake patterns significantly improves sleep quality, reduces sedative requirements, lowers delirium incidence, and shortens mechanical ventilation duration, demonstrating a favorable safety profile in mechanically ventilated patients.
papers.journal: Journal of clinical neuroscience : official journal of the Neurosurgical Society of Australasia

papers.title: A stochastic neural mass model for typical rhythms during sleep-wake transitions: Insights into dynamics driven by auditory noise.
papers.abstract: Sleep-wake transitions are essential for normal brain function. Although auditory noise can trigger sleep-wake transitions, how it influences the neural dynamics underlying these transitions and associated EEG rhythms remains unclear. Here, we propose a stochastic neural mass model to investigate how auditory noise modulates shifts in typical EEG rhythms during sleep-wake transitions. The model integrates the intrinsic sleep-wake regulatory circuit with rhythm-generating mechanisms and incorporates Gaussian colored noise (GCN) to represent auditory noise. Numerical simulations combined with deterministic and stochastic bifurcation-related analyses are used to evaluate how noise intensity, correlation rate, and intrinsic regulatory parameters influence transitions between alpha waves and slow oscillations. The model reproduces characteristic EEG rhythms during sleep and wakefulness, namely slow oscillations and alpha waves, and shows that the system exhibits a bistable regime in which slow oscillation and alpha wave limit cycles coexist as distinct attractors, with GCN inducing transitions between them. Increasing noise intensity and correlation rate bias the system toward the alpha waves associated with wakefulness, whereas lower values favor the slow oscillations associated with sleep. In addition, variations in intrinsic sleep-wake regulatory parameters reshape the basins of attraction of attractors, thereby modulating susceptibility to GCN-induced transitions. These results provide a model-based dynamical explanation for how auditory noise may modulate switching between typical EEG rhythm patterns associated with sleep-wake transitions and a reduced computational framework for investigating how auditory noise interacts with intrinsic neural regulation to influence sleep-wake rhythms. The framework may support future studies on sleep-wake regulation.
papers.journal: Computer methods and programs in biomedicine

papers.title: Temporal evolution of EEG hallmarks in childhood Lennox-Gastaut syndrome.
papers.abstract: The temporal development of generalized paroxysmal fast activity (GPFA) and slow spike-and-wave complexes in childhood Lennox-Gastaut syndrome (LGS) remains poorly characterized. This study mapped the emergence and longitudinal evolution of these EEG hallmarks in a real-world LGS cohort. This retrospective observational cohort study was conducted at a tertiary pediatric neurophysiology and neurology center. Patients aged 1-18 years fulfilling current International League Against Epilepsy criteria for LGS were identified through local databases. All available sleep video-EEG recordings before November 2024 were reviewed; clinical features, EEG findings, and comorbidities were collected at each recording. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. We reviewed 234 EEGs from 51 patients (75% male). Median age at first EEG was 5 years. GPFA emerged later than slow spike-and-wave (mean age: 9.6 vs 8.3 years, p = 0.002), with non-parametric analysis confirming a significant difference in age at first detection (p = 0.004). Median age at epilepsy onset was 1.1 years, while all clinical and EEG criteria for LGS were met at a median age of 10.9 years. EEG hallmarks of LGS emerged progressively during childhood, with slow spike-and-wave preceding GPFA during sleep. Following early clinical manifestations, a prolonged developmental phase may precede full electroclinical expression of LGS, with implications for early diagnosis and longitudinal EEG surveillance.

papers.title: CMAP as an electrophysiological biomarker in spinal muscular atrophy: A systematic review.
papers.abstract: To appraise the evidence on compound muscle action potential (CMAP) as a biomarker in spinal muscular atrophy (SMA): responsiveness to therapy, correlation with motor function, diagnosis and prognostic value, and patterns across SMA types. Conducted per PRISMA 2020 (PROSPERO CRD420261476823). PubMed and Embase were searched to August 15, 2026 for studies reporting CMAP in genetically confirmed SMA. Findings were synthesized narratively across four pre-specified domains using a Synthesis Without Meta-analysis approach. Two reviewers independently assessed risk of bias with Joanna Briggs Institute tools. Sixty-two studies (2513 participants across reports) were included. Following disease-modifying therapy, CMAP increased in 22 of 33 contributing studies (66.7%), was stable in 9 (27.3%), and showed a mixed pattern in 2 (6.1%); none reported a net decrease. All three disease-modifying therapies were associated with CMAP increase. CMAP correlated moderately to strongly with motor function scales and discriminated diagnostic or severity categories in 6 of the 11 studies that formally tested this. Risk of bias was low or low-moderate in 27 studies; small sample size and absence of a concurrent control group were the most frequent limitations. CMAP rises in roughly two-thirds of treated cohorts and reflects disease severity, but floor, ceiling, and site-dependent effects limit its use as a standalone surrogate endpoint. Selecting the recording site by severity, adding a second site chosen on the same basis, and agreeing standardized acquisition and normative values would strengthen its role as a prognostic stratifier and a component of multimodal models.

papers.title: Guided insertion of transfacial pin for early midface distraction in syndromic craniosynostosis: a retrospective cohort study.
papers.abstract: Syndromic craniosynostosis presents with premature fusion of multiple calvarial sutures including the skull base. This could result in severe mid-face retrusion, exorbitism, obstructive sleep apnea and elevated intracranial pressure (ICP). Fronto-orbital advancement or posterior calvarial vault distraction is performed early to reduce ICP, while the midface is handled later to ensure stability and reduce the frequency of interventions. Severe airway and ocular complications necessitate early midface advancement preferably using distraction. This study aims to assess outcomes and safety of early midface distraction (EMD) using guided transfacial pin fixation (GTP) in young individuals. A retrospective cohort study was conducted of all transfacial pin fixated midface distraction surgeries performed by a single surgeon between 2014 and 2024. Data reviewed included demographics, attempts required for pin insertion, accuracy of pin insertion, deviation from desired path, magnitude of distraction, functional outcome involving airway, globe position and complications. Fourteen patients underwent transfacial pin fixated midface distraction of which 6 involved use of 3D printed guides. The mean age was 4.3 years. All patients had significant obstructive sleep apnea and exorbitism. C-arm radiography was used as a standard monitoring aid irrespective of the use of guides. Twelve patients had undergone fronto-orbital advancement prior to midface advancement. We encountered minor intra-operative complication involving transfacial pin in 1 patient. Use of 3D printed guide appears to be safe and effective method for insertion of transfacial pins in centers which do not employ robotic assistance.
papers.journal: Journal of cranio-maxillo-facial surgery : official publication of the European Association for Cranio-Maxillo-Facial Surgery

papers.title: How School-Based Interventions Shape the Developing Brain during 3-12 Years: A Systematic Review and Exploratory Meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: The effects of school-based interventions (SBIs) on children's neurodevelopment are poorly synthesized. This systematic review integrates neuroscientific evidence on how structured educational activities influence brain development in children aged 3-12 years. Following PRISMA guidelines, we identified 17 empirical studies (published 2014-2025) using functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), electroencephalography (EEG), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), or magnetoencephalography (MEG). Of these, 8 studies were included in a random-effects meta-analysis and all 17 in a thematic synthesis. The meta-analysis revealed a preliminary association between SBIs and reduced amygdala activity during stress regulation tasks (r = -.28, 95% CI [-.50, -.02]), based on two studies, which should be interpreted as exploratory rather than confirmatory. No significant pooled effect for executive function, likely due to high heterogeneity. Thematic analysis distinguishes between mechanisms of plasticity and markers of intervention effectiveness: the first three characterize intra-individual mechanisms of experience-dependent plasticity, including (1) executive function interventions engaged prefrontal networks through both increased recruitment and enhanced neural efficiency; (2) socio-emotional programs modulated limbic-prefrontal circuits; (3) language and auditory programs shaped sensory-specific electrophysiological markers and cortical specialization; and the fourth theme identifies a neural marker of the effective process of intervention delivery, demonstrating that (4) teacher-child inter-brain synchrony was positively correlated with learning outcomes. By integrating findings across neural, cognitive, and affective domains, this review provides a conceptual framework linking pedagogical practices to neural plasticity and advances the understanding of the neurofunctional pathways through which educational experiences shape the developing brain.

papers.title: Visual-linguistic cues in manual communication: Neural and behavioral responses to Mouthings in sign-naïve perception.
papers.abstract: Gesture serves as a foundational modality for conveying event structure, providing critical visual information about transitivity and participant roles. Sign languages integrate manual (hand-based) and non-manual (face, torso, head) articulations to encode complex linguistic information. Among these, mouth movements provide phonological and lexical cues, but their role in sign-naïve individuals remains underexplored. This study investigates how sign-naïve individuals process non-manual markers (mouthings) in unfamiliar signed verbs, to explore how linguistic information is extracted from visual stimuli sharing properties with both gesture and sign language. Using EEG, we examined whether lip-reading functions as a linguistic cue or a general perceptual enhancement in non-signers viewing Austrian Sign Language (ÖGS) and non-ÖGS stimuli. Findings reveal distinct neural signatures for manual signs presented with and without congruent mouthings. An early posterior negativity followed by a late posterior positivity suggests that mouthings facilitate lexical access by providing phonological cues that activate stored lexical representations. Conversely, stimuli without mouthings elicited increased anterior activity, reflecting heightened cognitive control demands. Further, telic verbs, which inherently encode event endpoints, showed earlier and stronger facilitation from congruent mouthings compared to atelic verbs. These findings align with the Event Visibility Hypothesis and reinforce the role of visual cues in linguistic comprehension.

papers.title: Beyond the neurological horizon: A metabolic paradigm shift in intravenous iron therapy for restless legs syndrome.
papers.abstract: Intravenous (IV) iron therapy has substantially advanced the therapeutic landscape of Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS), offering potent disease-modifying benefits by directly addressing the central pathophysiology of brain iron deficiency. Consequently, ferric carboxymaltose (FCM) has rapidly emerged as the preferred formulation within sleep medicine, championed for its robust neurological efficacy and administration convenience. However, an interdisciplinary evaluation reveals a critical metabolic blind spot: FCM's unique propensity to induce intact fibroblast growth factor 23 (iFGF23)-mediated hypophosphatemia. While sleep specialists frequently dismiss this complication as a transient laboratory anomaly, extensive hematological evidence demonstrates that it precipitates severe, prolonged metabolic derangements, including osteomalacia, pathological fractures, and profound muscle weakness that clinically mimics RLS exacerbation. This perspective advocates for a paradigm shift in neuro-nutrition and sleep medicine, urging a targeted transition toward safer, equally efficacious alternatives, notably ferric derisomaltose (FDI), ferumoxytol, and low molecular weight iron dextran (LMW ID). By implementing a personalized, risk-stratified decision algorithm, clinicians can harmonize the neurological objectives of RLS treatment with the imperative of systemic metabolic safety.

papers.title: Modified sleep stage sequence analysis based on the stage immediately preceding each REM sleep period during nocturnal polysomnography to identify candidates for narcolepsy workup.
papers.abstract: To evaluate whether a modified sleep stage sequence (SSS) method based on a single epoch immediately preceding each rapid eye movement (REM) sleep period during nocturnal polysomnography (nPSG) could help identify candidates for further narcolepsy workup. This study retrospectively analyzed 204 participants: 39 with narcolepsy type 1 (NT1), 63 with narcolepsy type 2 (NT2), 62 with idiopathic hypersomnia (IH), and 40 healthy controls (HC). In nPSG, REM periods were classified by the single 30-s epoch immediately preceding their onset, excluding sleep-onset REM periods (SOREMPs). The participant-level SSS(W/N1) ratio was the proportion of remaining REM periods preceded by wakefulness or N1. Decision trees distinguished NT1/NT2 from IH/HC using REM sleep latency (REML) alone or with this ratio, with 50 stratified 70/30 hold-out splits for internal validation. In pooled multiple sleep latency test SOREMPs, the proposed method showed the same between-group ordering as conventional SSS. In pooled nocturnal REM periods excluding SOREMPs, the frequency of SSS(W/N1) was highest in NT1 and showed a stepwise numerical gradient across NT1, NT2, IH, and HC. Adding the SSS(W/N1) ratio to REML increased the median validation area under the receiver operating characteristic curve from 0.64 [interquartile range, 0.63-0.67] to 0.70 [0.68-0.74]. Two rounded high-specificity rules were derived: Rule A (REML-based), REML < 40 min; and Rule B (SSS-enhanced), SSS(W/N1) ratio ≥ 0.4 with REML < 125 min. Median sensitivity/specificity were 23%/98% and 37%/97%, respectively. A modified pre-REM SSS measure derived from routine nPSG may help prioritize patients for further narcolepsy workup.

papers.title: Slower growth, indoor environmental enrichment, or covered veranda access: A comparison of three rearing systems for broiler chicken welfare and behavior.
papers.abstract: The use of slower-growing chicken strains and environmental enrichments are major levers for improving broiler welfare. This study compared the effects of three rearing systems on the welfare and behavior of broiler chickens: intermediate-growing broilers (Redbro) kept in an unenriched environment ("RDB"), fast-growing broilers (Ross 308) kept in a highly enriched and complex indoor environment ("RoE+"), and fast-growing broilers (Ross 308) having access to a 36-m² covered veranda from D14 ("RoCV"). Each of the four 81-m² pens per treatment housed 1,350 birds until they reached a final body weight of 1.9 kg, corresponding to a final indoor stocking density of 30 kg/m². As they aged, the RoCV chickens increasingly went into the covered verandas until an average of 27% of the birds in the verandas was reached on D32. At the same time, RoE+ broilers perched more and more on the enrichments over time. RoE+ birds consumed more water than RoCV chickens from D24 onward, without any difference in feed consumption. RDB and RoCV birds had fewer leg lesions than RoE+ ones, although the litter quality did not differ between the treatments, but RDB birds had better gait scores than either RoE+ or RoCV broilers. More walking, running, foraging, sparring and frolicking behaviors were observed in the covered verandas than in the indoor pens, where resting behavior was more frequently observed. RoE+ birds dustbathed more often than RDB and RoCV chickens. No difference between treatments was found for mortality. Fewer RoCV broilers reached the different steps of the detour test and approached a novel object than RDB and RoE+ broilers. Overall, the three rearing systems compared influenced different aspects of broiler welfare: RDB treatment was associated with better walking ability and fewer occurrences of footpad dermatitis, RoE+ with more comfort behaviors, and RoCV with more active behaviors and improved footpad condition.

papers.title: Sex- and gender-related differences in narcolepsy and idiopathic hypersomnia: a narrative review.
papers.abstract: Sex- and gender-related differences are increasingly recognised across central disorders of hypersomnolence, although evidence varies between narcolepsy type 1, narcolepsy type 2 and idiopathic hypersomnia. Literature suggests females experience longer diagnostic delays in narcolepsy and are more frequently diagnosed with idiopathic hypersomnia. Females also report greater subjective sleepiness, poorer quality of life and higher rates of psychiatric comorbidity, whereas males may experience greater impacts on personal relationships and higher rates of suicidality. Preclinical studies demonstrate sex-specific differences in the orexin system, stress responses, energy metabolism and neuroendocrine regulation, providing plausible mechanisms for clinical heterogeneity; however, human evidence remains limited and inconsistent. Sex-related differences in objective sleep testing and treatment response have been reported, although few studies were designed to evaluate these outcomes. Women face additional management challenges related to pregnancy, contraception and medication safety as reproductive safety data remain limited for many wake-promoting and anti-cataplectic therapies. Overall, substantial evidence gaps remain, particularly for narcolepsy type 2 and idiopathic hypersomnia. Future prospective, sex-stratified studies and objective biomarkers capable of identifying biologically meaningful disease subtypes are needed to improve diagnosis, refine disease classification and support personalised management.

papers.title: Multi-layer analysis of gut metagenomic functional potential in major depressive disorder.
papers.abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is associated with gut microbiota dysbiosis, but previous studies have mostly focused on species composition and are subject to confounding factors such as age and diet. Robust differences at the functional pathway level remain unclear. We included 98 indigenous residents of Xinjiang, China, whose families had resided there for three or more generations (49 MDD patients and 49 healthy controls) and performed shotgun metagenomic sequencing. Functional profiles were annotated with HUMAnN3 across seven levels: GBM, GMM, KO, EC, Module, Pathway, and PathAbundance. Features were transformed using the centered log-ratio (CLR) method. After controlling for 10 covariates (age, sex, BMI, bowel movement frequency, diet, gastrointestinal symptoms, years of smoking, alcohol consumption, physical activity, and sleep), OLS regression was performed with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction (q < 0.05). Complementary analysis was conducted using MaAsLin2, together with age caliper matching (52 participants), recurrent/first-episode subgroup analyses, and sensitivity analyses for treatment history. Overall functional profiles were evaluated by PERMANOVA based on Aitchison distance. After covariate adjustment, overall functional profiles did not differ significantly between groups (PERMANOVA R²=1.9%, p = 0.071; PERMDISP p = 0.98). After FDR correction, 33 significant features were detected across five levels: EC, Pathway, Module, GMM, and PathAbundance (no significant signals at the GBM or KO levels). Key biologically meaningful signals included: propionate CoA-transferase (EC 2.8.3.1, β=-1.42, q = 0.022)↓, teichoic acid biosynthesis (map00552, β=-0.34, q = 0.045)↓, vancomycin resistance module (M00651, β=-1.28, q = 0.014)↓, galacturonate degradation II (MF0023, β=+1.82, q = 0.048)↑, and heme b biosynthesis I (PathAbundance, β=+0.93, q = 0.033)↑. MaAsLin2 effect sizes were correlated with the main OLS results at the Pathway level (R²=0.84) with consistent direction. GRSA independently confirmed downregulation of the phosphotransferase system (map02060, padj<0.001) and teichoic acid biosynthesis. The propionate CoA-transferase and teichoic acid biosynthesis signals were directionally consistent in the main model and recurrent subgroup, but did not survive correction in the matched subset; the first-episode subgroup (n = 11) was underpowered and its results are reported as exploratory. Gut microbiota functional potential in MDD patients shows a mild but directionally consistent shift after controlling for confounders, involving short-chain fatty acid production, Gram-positive bacterial cell wall metabolism, and cofactor metabolism. This study measures functional potential and requires validation by metabolomics.

papers.title: High Prevalence of Pruritus, Fatigue, and Sleep Disorders in MASLD Negatively Affects Health-related Quality of Life and Work Productivity.
papers.abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is associated with health-related quality of life (HRQL) impairment, which can be exacerbated by pruritus, fatigue, and/or sleep disorders. We assessed the prevalence of significant pruritus, fatigue, and sleep disorders in patients with MASLD and evaluated their association with HRQL and work productivity loss. Patients with MASLD were prospectively enrolled into the Global NAFLD/MASLD Registry. Clinical and HRQL (per CLDQ-MASH and WPAI:SHP questionnaires) data were analyzed according to the presence of significant pruritus, significant fatigue, and sleep disorders. A total of 8034 patients with MASLD from 39 countries (age 54±12 years, 46% male, 50% type 2 diabetes, 39% advanced fibrosis) were included. At baseline, 25% reported significant pruritus, 35% significant fatigue, and 34% sleep disorders, and 10% had all 3 symptoms. Patients with fatigue, pruritus, or sleep disorder were more likely to be female, have higher BMI, more metabolic comorbidities, and greater psychiatric burden. At 1-year follow-up, over half of the patients with baseline symptoms continued to experience them, and 14% to 18% developed de novo symptoms. Multivariate analyses showed that significant pruritus and sleep disorders each independently predicted fatigue [OR=9.51 (8.0-11.3)] when both conditions were present. Pruritus was a strong predictor of sleep disorders [OR=2.90 (2.6-3.3)]. All 3 conditions, especially fatigue, were independently associated with significantly impaired HRQL and work productivity loss. Clinically significant fatigue, pruritus, and sleep disorders are common in MASLD, having a negative impact on HRQL and a substantial economic burden.

papers.title: Gut Microbiota in Alzheimer's Disease and Healthy Aging: Mechanisms, Prevention Strategies and Healthcare Burden.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by cognitive decline associated with oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, tau neurofibrillary tangles, amyloid-beta plaque deposition, and metabolic dysfunction. Increasing evidence suggests that the gut microbiota plays an important role in AD pathogenesis through the microbiota-gut-brain axis. This review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the role of the gut microbiota in AD and healthy aging, with a particular focus on microbiota-targeted preventive and therapeutic strategies and their potential to influence disease progression. Recent studies have demonstrated that alterations in gut microbial composition are closely associated with AD. Patients with AD commonly exhibit a reduced abundance of short-chain fatty acid-producing bacteria and an increased prevalence of lipopolysaccharide-producing taxa, supporting a mechanistic link between microbial dysbiosis, systemic inflammation, and neurodegeneration. Emerging evidence indicates that dietary patterns, prebiotics, probiotics, synbiotics, postbiotics, and microbiota-based therapies, including fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), may beneficially modulate gut microbial composition and influence AD-related pathophysiological processes. In addition, lifestyle factors such as sleep quality and physical activity have been increasingly recognized for their interactions with the gut-brain axis and their potential to affect cognitive health. Current evidence highlights the gut microbiota as a promising therapeutic target in AD prevention and management. Microbiota-directed interventions, together with healthy dietary and lifestyle modifications, may help attenuate neuroinflammation, improve metabolic homeostasis, and delay cognitive decline. Furthermore, given the substantial global economic burden of AD, microbiota-focused preventive strategies may contribute not only to improving clinical outcomes but also to reducing long-term healthcare and societal costs. Future longitudinal and interventional studies are needed to establish causal relationships and determine the efficacy of microbiota-based therapies in AD.

papers.title: Management of shift work disorder: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline.
papers.abstract: This guideline establishes recommendations for the treatment of SWD. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) commissioned a task force of experts in sleep and circadian medicine to develop recommendations and assign strengths based on a systematic review of the literature and an assessment of the evidence using the GRADE process. The task force summarized the relevant literature and the quality of evidence, the balance of benefits and harms, patient values and preferences, and resource use considerations supporting the recommendations. The AASM Board of Directors approved the final recommendations. The following recommendations are intended as a guide for clinicians in choosing specific treatment(s) for symptoms of excessive sleepiness and/or insomnia, and for circadian adaptation in adults with SWD. Each recommendation statement is assigned a strength (e.g., "Strong" or "Conditional"). For SWD, there were only "conditional" recommendations for or against (i.e., "We suggest…") and those requiring the clinician to use clinical knowledge and experience and consider the individual patient's values and preferences to determine the best course of action. Interventions in recommendation statements were compared to no treatment. Adults with SWD with symptoms of excessive sleepiness associated with work schedule: 1. In adults with SWD with excessive sleepiness, the AASM suggests the use of armodafinil or modafinil taken 30 to 60 minutes prior to the night shift over no armodafinil or modafinil (Conditional recommendation, moderate certainty of evidence). 2. In adults with SWD with excessive sleepiness, the AASM suggests the use of bright light over no bright light during the night shift (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). Individuals with SWD who exhibit insomnia and daytime function impairments may also benefit from using bright light during their night shift. 3. In adults with SWD with excessive sleepiness, the AASM suggests the use of caffeine taken prior to and/or during the night shift over no caffeine (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). Caffeine intake close to bedtime can disrupt sleep onset and quality, which may exacerbate symptoms of SWD. 4. In adults with SWD with excessive sleepiness, the AASM suggests the use of a clockwise rotating shift schedule over a counterclockwise rotating shift schedule (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). 5. In adults with SWD with excessive sleepiness, the AASM suggests taking a nap over no nap prior to the night shift (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). Sleep inertia occurring soon after the nap may temporarily increase sleepiness, decrease cognitive performance, and increase accident risk. Allowing adequate time for resolution of sleep inertia prior to driving or performing other safety-sensitive behaviors may be needed to reduce these risks. 6. In adults with SWD with excessive sleepiness, the AASM suggests either not eating or eating a snack rather than eating a full meal during the night shift (Conditional recommendation, low certainty of evidence). 7. In adults with SWD with excessive sleepiness, the AASM suggests the combination of caffeine and bright light over the combination of no caffeine and no bright light (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). Caffeine intake close to bedtime can disrupt sleep onset and quality, which may exacerbate symptoms of SWD. 8. In adults with SWD with excessive sleepiness, the AASM suggests the combination of taking a nap and caffeine over the combination of no nap and no caffeine prior to the night shift (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). Adults with SWD with sleep disturbance/insomnia: 9. In adults with SWD with daytime sleep disturbance/insomnia the AASM suggests the use of CBT-I over no CBT-I (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). 10. In adults with SWD with daytime sleep disturbance/insomnia following the night shift, the AASM suggests the use of melatonin over no melatonin (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). 11. In adults with SWD with sleep disturbance/insomnia, when transitioning from daytime to nighttime sleep, the AASM suggests the use of melatonin over no melatonin for night sleep following shift work (Conditional recommendation, low certainty of evidence). 12. In adults with SWD who desire to take a nap prior to the first night shift, the AASM suggests the use of melatonin over no melatonin prior to the nap (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). Melatonin may temporarily increase sleepiness, decrease cognitive performance, and increase accident risk. Allowing adequate time for resolution of sleepiness prior to driving, returning to work or performing other safety-sensitive behaviors may be needed to reduce these risks. 13. In adults with SWD with daytime sleep disturbance/insomnia, the AASM suggests the use of ramelteon or other melatonin receptor agonists over no melatonin receptor agonist (Conditional recommendation, low certainty of evidence). 14. In adults with SWD with daytime sleep disturbance/insomnia, the AASM suggests the use of suvorexant or other dual orexin receptor antagonists over no dual orexin receptor antagonists (Conditional recommendation, low certainty of evidence). 15. In adults with SWD with daytime sleep disturbance/insomnia, the AASM suggests against the use of triazolam and other benzodiazepines (conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). Adults with SWD seeking circadian adaptation: 16. In adults with SWD seeking circadian adaptation to the night shift, the AASM suggests the use of bright light over no bright light during the night shift (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty). For individuals who work rotating or frequently changing shifts, circadian adaptation is not a realistic goal of treatment and therefore they would not be expected to benefit from this intervention. The evidence supporting this recommendation came from studies in which individuals reached partial circadian adaptation to the night shift. 17. In adults with SWD seeking circadian adaptation to the night shift, the AASM suggests the combination of bright light at night and fixed daytime sleep timing over the combination of no bright light and no fixed sleep timing (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). For individuals who work rotating or frequently changing shifts, circadian adaptation is not a realistic goal of treatment and therefore they would not be expected to benefit from this intervention. The evidence supporting this recommendation came from studies in which individuals reached partial circadian adaptation to the night shift. 18. In adults with SWD seeking circadian adaptation to the night shift, the AASM suggests the combination of bright light at night, fixed daytime sleep timing, and reduced-light-transmittance glasses in the morning over the combination of no bright light, no fixed sleep timing, and no reduced-light-transmittance glasses (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). Remark 1 : For individuals who work rotating or frequently changing shifts, circadian adaptation is not a realistic goal of treatment and therefore they would not be expected to benefit from this intervention. The evidence supporting this recommendation came from studies in which individuals reached partial circadian adaptation to the night shift. Remark 2: Attention to driving safety is important when wearing reduced-light-transmittance glasses. Other considerations for adults with SWD: 19. In adults with SWD who are working either an 8-hour or 12-hour night shift, the AASM does not suggest working one shift duration over the other (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). This recommendation does not consider other shift durations, rotation, or the number of consecutive shifts. This guideline did not look at shift durations exceeding 12 hours. The total number of hours worked per week ranged from 36 to 52.

papers.title: Management of shift work disorder: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine systematic review, meta-analysis, and GRADE assessment.
papers.abstract: The purpose of this systematic review is to provide supporting evidence for a clinical practice guideline on the treatment of adults with shift work disorder (SWD). The American Academy of Sleep Medicine commissioned a task force of six experts in sleep and circadian medicine. A systematic review was conducted to identify randomized controlled trials, observational studies, and treatment trials in which treatments for the symptoms of excessive sleepiness and/or sleep disturbance/insomnia in adults with SWD, and for circadian adaptation to shift work schedules was tested. Evidence from controlled laboratory trials of simulated shift work and of field-based trials of shift workers with and without a diagnosis of SWD was included. Statistical analyses were performed to determine the significance of critical and important outcomes and clinically meaningful thresholds were set to determine the clinical relevance of treatments on the outcomes examined, where possible. Finally, the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) process was used to assess the evidence for making recommendations. The literature search resulted in 3,045 articles; 118 studies provided data suitable for statistical analyses. The task force provided a detailed summary of the evidence along with the quality of evidence, the balance of benefits and harms, patient values and preferences, and resource use considerations.

papers.title: The Interplay Between Depression and Cardiovascular Disease: Mechanisms, Clinical Implications, and Emerging Therapeutic Perspectives.
papers.abstract: Depression and cardiovascular disease (CVD) frequently co-occur and contribute substantially to global morbidity and mortality. This narrative review synthesizes current evidence on the biological, psychological, and clinical mechanisms connecting these two conditions. The aim is to clarify the key pathways underlying their bidirectional relationship and to highlight therapeutic strategies that may improve outcomes in individuals affected by both disorders. Recent studies increasingly demonstrate that depression and CVD share multifaceted biological mechanisms, including hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis dysregulation, systemic inflammation, autonomic imbalance, oxidative stress, endothelial dysfunction, and genetic and epigenetic alterations. Immunological activity, particularly cytokine-mediated neuroinflammation, has emerged as a central component linking mood dysregulation with vascular pathology. Behavioral and psychosocial pathways also contribute to cardiovascular risk. Adverse health behaviors, including physical inactivity, poor diet, smoking, substance use, sleep disturbance, and treatment nonadherence, may directly contribute to cardiovascular risk, while psychosocial factors such as chronic stress and social isolation may influence or amplify these behavioral and biological pathways. Additionally, precision-medicine strategies that incorporate genetic, metabolic, and psychosocial profiles are increasingly recognized as important for optimizing individualized care. Depression and CVD are interconnected through a complex web of biological and psychosocial pathways that mutually reinforce disease progression. Understanding these shared mechanisms is critical for improving prevention, diagnosis, and treatment. Integrated, multidisciplinary management, addressing inflammation, autonomic dysfunction, lifestyle factors, and mental health, is essential to reduce morbidity in this high-risk population. Future research should continue exploring biomarkers and personalized interventions to better manage this intertwined comorbidity.

papers.title: Exposomic Determinants in Heart Failure Among Older Adults - Mechanistic Links, Clinical Evidence, and Future Perspectives.
papers.abstract: Heart failure (HF) in older adults emerges from the interplay between biological aging and the totality of environmental and behavioural exposures conceptualized as the exposome. Traditional cardiovascular risk factors and intrinsic cardiac pathology only partially explain HF burden, as chronic exposures to air pollution, traffic noise, temperature extremes, toxic metals and chemicals, artificial light at night, and adverse social environments, along with low greenness and walkability, substantially influence HF incidence, decompensations, and prognosis in older patients with multiple comorbidities. Recently, epidemiological studies have associated many of the exposomic factors with HF incidence and morbidity. Age‑related impairments of the myocardium and vasculature make them particularly vulnerable to external stressors. Mechanistically, aging, HF, and environmental factors converge on shared pathways including, oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammaging, impaired autophagy and proteostasis, genomic and epigenetic alterations, cellular senescence, dysregulated neurohormonal and circadian signalling, and fibrosis with maladaptive remodelling. Through these mechanisms exposome chronically accelerates cardiovascular aging and lowers the threshold for HF onset and progression. This review considers a shift from an organ‑centred view of HF in older adults to a systems‑level, life‑course perspective that explicitly incorporates exposomic determinants, and argues that reducing harmful exposures while promoting green space, physical activity, walkability, and healthy dietary patterns should be integral to HF prevention and management strategies in aging societies.

papers.title: Copy number variants across the developmental epilepsy-developmental and epileptic encephalopathy spectrum: an Indonesian case series.
papers.abstract: Developmental epilepsy (DE) and developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE) comprise neurodevelopmental disorders in which epilepsy occurs alongside developmental impairment of varying contributions from the underlying etiology and epileptic activity. Advances in genetic testing, including whole-exome sequencing (WES), whole-genome sequencing (WGS), and chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA), have facilitated the identification of copy number variants (CNVs); however, data on CNV-associated epilepsy and neurodevelopmental disorders remain limited in Southeast Asia, including Indonesia. This retrospective case series describes the clinical and genetic characteristics of four Indonesian children across the DE-DEE spectrum with pathogenic CNVs identified at a tertiary referral hospital in Yogyakarta, Indonesia. Among 48 patients who underwent WES, CNVs were identified in five; four underwent further genetic characterization and were included in this case series, while one patient died before additional testing could be performed. Clinical manifestations included early-onset seizures, developmental delay or intellectual impairment, and abnormal EEG and/or neuroimaging findings. Genetic findings included a 2q24.3 deletion involving SCN1A in a patient with Dravet syndrome and 15q11.2-q13.1 deletions involving UBE3A in three patients with clinical features of Angelman syndrome. Confirmatory testing using WGS or CMA further characterized the identified CNVs. This case series expands the clinical and molecular data on pathogenic CNVs associated with pediatric epilepsy and neurodevelopmental disorders in an underrepresented Southeast Asian population and illustrates the complementary roles of sequencing and chromosomal analysis in genetic diagnosis.

papers.title: Sleep deprivation disrupts error awareness and subsequent behavioural regulation.
papers.abstract: Sleep deprivation is known to impair cognitive performance, yet its effects on error awareness and subsequent behavioural adjustments remain incompletely understood. Here, we investigated how sleep loss affects the use of subjective performance evaluation to guide post-error adaptations. Thirty healthy adults completed a novel, gamified error awareness multi-rule Simon task once while well rested and once after one night of total sleep deprivation. On each trial, participants reported both their task response and subjective evaluation of response accuracy. This design allowed us to dissociate objective performance from subjective error awareness and to examine their influence on subsequent behaviour over time. Sleep deprivation slowed responses, reduced accuracy, increased missed responses, and decreased the proportion of consciously detected errors, with impairments increasing over time on task. Both objective errors and subjective error judgements were associated with subsequent slowing. When well rested, subjective-error-associated slowing exceeded objective-error-associated slowing. This difference was reduced under sleep deprivation. Specifically, objectively correct responses judged as errors were followed by slowing relative to correctly judged correct responses, and this slowing was attenuated under sleep deprivation. Accuracy showed post-error decreases that were most pronounced following objective errors. Together, the findings indicate that sleep deprivation reduces error awareness and is associated with altered post-error behavioural regulation.

papers.title: Low Frequency of Sexual Intercourse, Discrepancy Between Erectile Function Measures, and Sexual Satisfaction Among Japanese Men Aged 45-64 Years: A Nationwide Cross-Sectional Study.
papers.abstract: To examine sexual behavior, erectile function, and sexual satisfaction among middle-aged Japanese men using nationwide survey data. This secondary analysis used data from a 2023 nationwide online survey of male sexual dysfunction in Japan. Men aged 45-64 years were included. Sexual behavior was assessed by frequencies of sexual intercourse and masturbation. Erectile function was assessed using the Sexual Health Inventory for Men (SHIM) and Erection Hardness Score (EHS), with ED defined as EHS ≤ 2. Sexual satisfaction was assessed using the overall satisfaction domain of the International Index of Erectile Function. Multivariable logistic regression identified factors associated with ED. Overall, 2314 men were analyzed (mean age, 53.8 ± 5.6 years). Sexual intercourse was infrequent: 48.1% reported intercourse less than once per year and 35.1% within the past 6 months, whereas 45.9% reported masturbation once or twice weekly. ED prevalence differed substantially by assessment method: 82.1% according to SHIM versus 26.9% according to EHS. Men with EHS-defined ED had significantly lower overall sexual satisfaction scores than those without ED (p < 0.001), although satisfaction scores substantially overlapped. Older age, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, mental illness, and sleep apnea syndrome were independently associated with ED. Among middle-aged Japanese men, the prevalence of ED varied substantially according to the assessment method, while EHS-defined ED was associated with lower overall sexual satisfaction despite substantial overlap in satisfaction scores. These findings support considering both erectile function and subjective sexual satisfaction when assessing sexual health.

papers.title: Longitudinal associations between sleep disturbance and disordered eating: the mediating role of emotion dysregulation.
papers.abstract: Accruing evidence suggests a significant relationship between sleep disturbances and disordered eating. Early adolescence is a period of heightened vulnerability for sleep disturbances and disordered eating. However, the longitudinal relationship between sleep disturbance and disordered eating remains unclear in early adolescent samples. The current study aims to examine if sleep disturbance longitudinally predicts disordered eating in early adolescents 3 years later, how the odds of having clinically significant disordered eating change per each unit increase in sleep disturbance, and if emotion dysregulation mediates these relationships. A sample of 6,161 early adolescents between 9 and 13 years old from the Adolescent Brain and Cognitive DevelopmentSM Study (ABCD Study®) was examined with data extracted from baseline, 2-year follow-up, and 3-year follow-up. Participants who completed Kiddie Schedule for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia, Computerized Version (KSADS-COMP), Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL), and Sleep Disturbance Scale for Children (SDSC) were included. A binary clinically significant disordered eating variable was created by coding participants who met criteria for present, past, or partial remission eating disorder diagnoses on the KSADS-5. Results indicated that greater sleep disturbance at baseline was associated with higher levels of disordered eating and clinically significant disordered eating at 3-year follow-up, and emotion dysregulation partially mediated these relationships (all ps < .001). Given that sleep is a modifiable factor, these results underscore the potential for integrating sleep-focused interventions into ED prevention and treatment programs for early adolescents. Interventions targeting emotion regulation may help reduce the impact of sleep problems on disordered eating in early adolescents.

papers.title: Developmental mechanisms contributing to non-linear firing dynamics in spinal motoneurons of the postnatal mouse.
papers.abstract: The intrinsic properties of spinal motoneurons support flexible movement, including the maintenance of postural tone. Motoneurons can produce sustained action potential output that outlasts synaptic input, a phenomenon traditionally attributed to persistent inward currents (PICs) mediated by sodium and calcium channels. Using whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiology, we examined how specific ion channels contribute to PIC maturation and non-linear firing dynamics that allow motoneurons to sustain their output in fast and slow lumbar motoneurons across postnatal development in mice. PIC amplitude and non-linear firing dynamics increased after weight-bearing in fast but not slow motoneurons. Blocking NaV1.6 channels reduced PIC amplitude at both pre- and post-weight-bearing stages, whereas L-type calcium channel blockade only reduced PICs after weight-bearing emerged. However, reducing PIC amplitude by blocking these channels, either individually or in parallel, did not abolish sustained firing hysteresis, which may be because PICs are not yet fully established at this stage of postnatal development. Unexpectedly, activation of muscarinic receptors increased PIC amplitude while promoting adaptive firing dynamics, suggesting that PICs alone do not account for sustained firing hysteresis. We also found that pharmacological manipulation of potassium currents mediated by KCNQ and KV1.2 channels produced substantial changes in firing dynamics. Strikingly, blocking hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated channels promoted sustained firing dynamics and led to the emergence of self-sustained firing in fast motoneurons. These results indicate that PICs and non-linear firing dynamics mature together and extend the current framework on non-linear firing dynamics of motoneurons to include additional voltage-gated ion channels. KEY POINTS: Persistent inward currents (PICs) and recruitment-derecruitment hysteresis increase in parallel in fast, but not slow, motoneurons following the onset of hindlimb weight-bearing. Increased expression or function of L-type calcium channels may contribute to enhanced PIC amplitude in fast motoneurons after weight-bearing emerges. Blocking NaV1.6 or L-type calcium channels did not reduce sustained firing hysteresis in fast motoneurons. KCNQ channels oppose PICs and, together with KV1.2 channels, shape recruitment-derecruitment asymmetry, thereby modulating firing hysteresis in fast motoneurons. Hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated channels generate a resting H-current that delays recruitment, modulates firing hysteresis, and prevents the emergence of self-sustained firing in fast motoneurons.

Tonakiamides A and B, Antitrypanosomal Lipopeptides Isolated from a Marine Okeania sp. Cyanobacterium.
papers.abstract: The structure elucidation of peptidic natural products is often hindered by extensive N-methylation and repetitive sequence motifs, which complicate NMR spectral analysis. Tonakiamides A and B (1 and 2), two lipopeptides isolated from a marine Okeania sp. cyanobacterium collected in Japan, represent such challenging compounds. Tonakiamides A and B (1 and 2) are acyclic nonapeptides composed of a hexanoic acid moiety and nine amino acid residues, six of which are N-methylated, resulting in complex mixtures of rotamers. Their structures were elucidated through a combination of spectroscopic and spectrometric analyses together with the characterization of three partial hydrolysates obtained under mild hydrolysis conditions. Tonakiamides A and B exhibited moderate growth-inhibitory activities against Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense, the causative agent of African sleeping sickness.

papers.title: When Menstrual Pain Becomes Care-Worthy: A Qualitative Study of Delayed Care-Seeking Among Young Women With Function-Limiting Dysmenorrhoea in Southwest China.
papers.abstract: Dysmenorrhoea can disrupt education, work, sleep, mobility and other daily activities, yet recurrent pain that limits daily functioning does not always prompt timely formal care-seeking. The aim of this study was to explore how young women in Southwest China interpret recurrent function-limiting dysmenorrhoea and decide whether to seek formal care. This qualitative study was based in Guiyang, Guizhou Province, Southwest China. Seventeen women aged 18-31 years with recurrent dysmenorrhoea affecting daily functioning took part in semi-structured interviews. Interviews were conducted face-to-face or online, audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Five themes were developed: making pain ordinary across family, peers and clinics; keeping pain within the logic of warmth and regulation; when pain becomes care-worthy: functional disruption as a threshold; reproductive expectations and delayed medicalisation; and normal tests, uncertain explanations and delayed re-entry into care. Care-seeking was often delayed as participants normalised menstrual pain, relied on culturally familiar warming or body-regulating practices, had concerns about analgesics or expected pain to improve after childbirth. Non-specific clinical explanations could also temporarily reassure participants and contribute to delay. Participants described seeking formal care when pain disrupted study, work, sleep, mobility or daily activities, when medication or self-management no longer worked, or when reproductive or gynaecological concerns emerged. Delayed care-seeking was shaped by whether menstrual pain became recognised as a legitimate reason for formal care. Menstrual health education and clinical communication should validate function-limiting pain, clarify when assessment is needed and provide clear follow-up guidance. Four women with lived experience of function-limiting dysmenorrhoea helped develop parts of the interview guide. Their feedback during pilot interviews led to additional questions about healthcare access and practical barriers to seeking care. They also supported recruitment and contributed to discussions of interview accounts and developing themes.
papers.journal: Health expectations : an international journal of public participation in health care and health policy

papers.title: Design of an adaptive lower limb rehabilitation system with virtual reality and multimodal biosignals.
papers.abstract: To develop and evaluate a virtual-reality-enhanced lower-limb rehabilitation framework that combines EEG-based motor-intention detection, robotic gait assistance, trunk-motion assessment, and lumbar surface electromyography to support multimodal assessment, interactive training, and therapist-oriented performance monitoring. Nine healthy participants completed VR-enhanced EEG motor-imagery training, open-loop calibration, closed-loop exoskeleton-triggering, trunk-attitude assessment, and lumbar-sEMG evaluation in separate experimental sessions. A four-degree-of-freedom hip-knee exoskeleton was integrated with participant-specific CDF threshold calibration, treadmill synchronization, VR rehabilitation tasks, attitude sensing, and RMS/MPF analysis. Participant identity was consistent across modalities, although the signals were not acquired simultaneously. The seated VR motor-imagery condition produced the highest open-loop command accuracy of 75.35 ± 4.21 %. Mean closed-loop gait-triggering accuracy was 76.7 ± 10.0 %, ranging from 60 % to 90 %. Mean trunk-movement magnitudes were 30.8°, 30.7°, 91.3°, and 31.0° for left lateral flexion, right lateral flexion, forward flexion, and backward extension, respectively. System prompting increased mean RMS from 0.094759 to 0.103330 mV and reduced mean MPF from 111.2023 to 103.0729 Hz. The findings support the feasibility of integrating intention-driven exoskeleton control, VR interaction, postural assessment, and muscular-response monitoring within a unified rehabilitation framework for adaptive, multimodal rehabilitation.

papers.title: Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea: Predictors of Surgical Success via Weighted Analysis.
