papers.title: The Sleep-Wake Classification Performance of Pediatric-Trained Machine Learning Algorithms for Raw Accelerometer Data.
papers.abstract: Actigraphy sleep-wake classification methods increasingly seek to leverage raw acceleration data and machine-learning-based classification, but performance evaluation in pediatrics is limited. We trained machine-learning models using pediatric data and compared their sleep-wake classification performance with existing algorithms for children. Sixty-five children (46% female, ages 5.3-17.7 years) completed in-lab overnight polysomnography and wore a GENEActiv device on their non-dominant wrist. The acceleration data were converted into 30-second epochs and aligned with physician-scored sleep-wake data from electroencephalography. Eight machine-learning models were trained using leave-one-subject-out cross-validation. Epoch-by-epoch analyses generated performance metrics (e.g., balanced accuracy [BA]) and discrepancy analyses provided overall sleep duration bias estimates. The combination of highest performance and least bias was used to rank using Euclidean distance scores - where a lower score represents closer to perfect performance and zero bias. For benchmarking, we included GGIR sleep scoring algorithms and an adult trained random forest classifier. Overall, 560.1 hours of polysomnography and actigraphy data were collected (74.4% of epochs were scored as sleep). The pediatric-trained local-global long-short term memory (LSTM) classifier had the most optimal epoch-by-epoch performance (e.g., BA=0.85, sensitivity=0.88, specificity=0.83, ROC-AUC=0.95, and Cohen's kappa=0.67). These metrics exceeded that of an adult-trained random forest classifier and GGIR-based algorithms. Discrepancy analyses revealed that overall sleep duration was underestimated by an average of 25 minutes using the LSTM classifier with no proportional bias. We trained eight pediatric sleep-wake classifiers that had a strong ability to detect sleep and wake, with the LSTM classifier being most optimal.

papers.title: Is adherence to the 24-hour movement guidelines related to a lower risk of cardiovascular events? A prospective cohort study including 13 897 participants from the SUN project.
papers.abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains the leading global cause of death, and preventive interventions are likely to be the most effective strategies. The 24-hour movement guidelines emphasize an integrated score, including physical activity (PA), sedentary time, and sleep. The combined effect of adhering to all three 24-hour movement guidelines on CVD events remains unclear. In a prospective assessment of 13 897 Spanish university graduates from the Seguimiento Universidad de Navarra cohort, the relationship between a comprehensive exposure (adherence to all three 24-hour movement guidelines) and CVD incidence was investigated. Participants completed baseline questionnaires from 1999, with biennial follow-up. Exposure was assessed using the Canadian 24-Hour Movement Guidelines: ≥ 150 minutes/week of moderate-to-vigorous PA, ≤ 8 hours/day sitting, and 7-9 hours/night sleep (or 7-8 hours for ≥ 65 years). A composite score (0-3 points) was calculated for the exposure. The primary endpoint was incident CVD (nonfatal myocardial infarction, stroke, cardiovascular death). Nearly half (46.68%) of participants met all three guidelines, while only 0.96% met none. Over a mean follow-up of 14.48 years, 148 cardiovascular event (CVE) occurred. Fully adjusted models revealed a significantly reduced CVE risk for participants meeting two [hazard ratio (HR) = 0.37; 95% confidence interval (CI): 0.14-0.99], or three (HR = 0.36; 95% CI: 0.14-0.95) guidelines compared to meeting none. Adherence to at least two of the 24-hour movement guidelines appears to be associated with a lower risk of CVEs. These findings suggest that a comprehensive approach to daily movement behaviors may play a beneficial role in CVD prevention. Public health strategies could consider promoting these integrated guidelines as part of broader efforts to improve cardiovascular health.

papers.title: Music-Based Intervention in Postoperative Lung Transplant Care: A Feasibility Study.
papers.abstract: Music-based interventions may support recovery in medical and surgical settings; however, their implementation during the immediate postoperative period following lung transplantation remains understudied. This single-center randomized feasibility study examined whether a structured music-based intervention delivered by board-certified music therapists could be implemented at clinically meaningful postoperative recovery milestones and explored preliminary trends in pain, anxiety, medication use, sleep, and length of stay. Twenty-nine adult lung transplant recipients (experimental n = 17, control n = 12) were enrolled between September 2021 and September 2023. Participants in the intervention group received music-based intervention sessions during spontaneous awakening trials, 24-48 hr following extubation, and within 72 hr of transfer from the intensive care unit to a step-down unit. Intervention components included patient-preferred live music, music-assisted relaxation, and optional receptive or active music engagement tailored to patient status. Intervention delivery was feasible across all three postoperative milestones, although challenges related to recruitment, retention, sleep measurement, and intervention standardization were identified. Exploratory analyses suggested lower observed pain scores and lower median acetaminophen use in the intervention group compared to standard care; however, no outcomes reached statistical significance. Anxiety outcomes did not differ between groups, and sleep measurement using consumer-grade wearable devices was not feasible. These findings support the feasibility of music-based interventions during postoperative lung transplant recovery and provide guidance for the design of future adequately powered trials using refined outcome measures, milestone-based intervention delivery, and improved implementation strategies.

papers.title: The mediating role of sleep blood pressure in the association between B-type natriuretic peptide and cardiovascular events: The Nagahama Study.
papers.abstract: B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) is a risk marker for not only heart failure but also cardiovascular diseases (CVD). This study investigated the possible mediating role of sleep blood pressure (BP) in the association between BNP and CVD events. Data for 5,751 participants were obtained from the Nagahama Study, a longitudinal cohort study of the general Japanese population. Circulating BNP levels were determined from blood specimens. BP was measured at home in the morning and evening, and three times per night during sleep using a timer-equipped cuff-oscillometric device. During the mean follow-up period of 9.4 years (54,350 person-years), 169 CVD cases were observed (Incidence rate: 31.1 per 10,000 person-year, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 26.7, 36.2). BNP levels ≥40 pg/mL were independently associated with CVD. The sleep BP-adjusted hazard ratio of high BNP for CVD was 1.80 (95% CI: 1.18, 2.74), while the awake home BP-adjusted hazard ratio was 1.92 (95% CI: 1.26, 2.91). Causal mediation analysis indicated a greater mediation rate of sleep SBP (14.3%, 95% CI: -2.8, 31.3) than awake home SBP (5.8%, 95% CI; -2.6, 14.2) in the association between BNP and CVD incidence. Factors associated with log-normalized BNP levels were age, sex, body mass index, sleep SBP, and nocturnal urination frequency. Prognostic significance of BNP for CVD events was partially mediated by BP particularly BP during sleep.

papers.title: Recognizing fibromyalgia-like pain phenotypes in lipedema: A narrative review.
papers.abstract: IntroductionLipedema is a chronic adipose and connective tissue disorder in which pain is classically localized to affected limb tissue. However, some patients report joint, periarticular, myotendinous, or axial pain, with fatigue, sleep disturbance, and exercise intolerance. When symptoms become widespread, the presentation may resemble fibromyalgia (FM), creating a diagnostic challenge for phlebologists.ObjectivesTo provide a clinical framework for distinguishing characteristic lipedema tissue pain from musculoskeletal pain generators, secondary central pain amplification, and potentially coexisting FM.MethodsThis narrative review was conducted with reference to the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA). PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar were searched through May 2026 for studies addressing lipedema, FM, widespread pain, hypermobility, connective tissue vulnerability, biomechanical dysfunction, and pain sensitization. Reference lists were manually screened. No formal risk-of-bias assessment or quantitative synthesis was performed.ResultsCharacteristic lipedema pain is predominantly localized to affected adipose tissue and associated with tenderness, pressure sensitivity, easy bruising, and functional impairment. Observational studies have also reported joint and periarticular pain, axial symptoms, hypermobility, and biomechanical dysfunction in patient subsets. Extra-adipose pain should be assessed separately and not automatically attributed either to lipedema or independent FM. Tissue hypersensitivity, stromal and microvascular alterations, joint instability, and altered biomechanics may represent peripheral pain generators contributing to secondary central amplification. However, observational evidence does not establish whether widespread pain is intrinsic to lipedema, secondary to musculoskeletal dysfunction or central amplification, or reflects coexisting FM.ConclusionsIn patients with lipedema and extra-adipose or widespread pain, phlebologists should assess joint hypermobility, instability, biomechanical dysfunction, and axial or musculoskeletal pain. FM criteria identify a widespread pain phenotype but cannot determine whether it represents an independent comorbidity or is related to persistent peripheral nociceptive mechanisms. Multidisciplinary assessment may improve diagnostic characterization and individualized management.

papers.title: Intersecting pathways of postpartum depressive symptoms and recurrent binge eating after gestational diabetes: Findings from the LINDA-Brazil cohort.
papers.abstract: To estimate the prevalence and correlates of recurrent binge eating (RBE) and postpartum depression (PPD), and examine their association among women with prior gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM). This cross-sectional analysis included 699 women with prior GDM who participated in the postpartum baseline assessment of the LINDA-Brazil study. RBE was defined as self-reported recurrent episodes of consuming large quantities of food within a discrete period, accompanied by a sense of lack of control during these episodes. PPD was measured using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS), with a cutoff score ≥13. Sociodemographic, obstetric, behavioral, and nutritional characteristics were obtained by interview. Associations were examined using Poisson regression models with robust variance. Among the 699 participants, 272 (38.9%) presented RBE, and 184 (26.3%) had PPD. At least one of the two outcomes was identified in 49.4% of participants, and 15.9% presented both. RBE was more prevalent among younger women and those with postpartum weight retention greater than 5 kg. PPD was associated with lower household income, current smoking, parity, weight-related factors, and poor sleep quality, whereas current breastfeeding was associated with a lower prevalence. In the primary analysis, women with RBE had a higher prevalence of PPD than women without RBE (prevalence ratio [PR], 2.17; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.63-2.88). RBE and PPD were common and frequently co-occurred among women with recent GDM. Women with RBE had approximately twice the prevalence of PPD compared with those without RBE. Longitudinal studies are needed to clarify the temporal relationship between these conditions.
papers.journal: International journal of gynaecology and obstetrics: the official organ of the International Federation of Gynaecology and Obstetrics

papers.title: Lifestyle Medicine in the 21st Century: Evidence-Based Strategies for Noncommunicable Disease Risk Reduction.
papers.abstract: Noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) account for over 74% of global mortality, with cardiovascular diseases, type 2 diabetes, cancers, and chronic respiratory diseases comprising the largest share. These conditions impose substantial health, social, and economic burdens worldwide, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. This narrative review synthesizes current evidence on the role of lifestyle medicine, a clinical discipline employing evidence-based lifestyle interventions in the prevention, management, and potential reversal of NCDs. Relevant randomized controlled trials, meta-analyses, and large-scale cohort studies were reviewed, focusing on the six core pillars of lifestyle medicine: optimal nutrition, regular physical activity, restorative sleep, effective stress management, avoidance of risky substances, and positive social connections. Robust evidence indicates that plant-based and Mediterranean dietary patterns, structured physical activity, adequate sleep, mindfulness-based stress reduction, tobacco avoidance, and fostering social connectedness significantly lower NCD incidence and progression. Advances in digital health, wearable devices, and precision-based strategies enhance personalization, monitoring, and adherence to lifestyle interventions. Persistent gaps include limited long-term adherence data, underrepresentation of diverse populations in clinical research, insufficient integration of sociocultural determinants, and lack of standardized implementation frameworks in healthcare systems. Lifestyle medicine provides a comprehensive, cost-effective approach to NCD prevention and control. Scaling culturally adaptable, technology-enabled, and equity-focused strategies is essential to establish lifestyle-based prevention as a global standard in combating the rising NCD epidemic.

papers.title: Work Schedules and Sleep Hours: a Synthesis of Select Guidelines and Recommendations to Reduce Fatigue-Related Risk in Mining and other Safety-Critical Sectors.
papers.abstract: Timing and duration of work can affect sleep opportunity and impact safety, with long hours prolonging exposure to fatigue risk factors, shortening sleep opportunities, and potentially misaligning natural sleep rhythms. These issues are especially relevant in the mining industry, where long working hours and continuous operations often require work outside a traditional 9-to-5 schedule. As a result, mine workers may face increased fatigue-risk, highlighting the importance of a fatigue-focused approach to work schedule design. This paper provides a synthesis of select work schedule and sleep duration recommendations relevant to industrial sectors like mining while contextualizing the results within the larger scope of fatigue risk management. A grey literature review identified 38 documents where the most common recommendations across documents, including those for the mining sector, were for shifts up to 12 h in duration with at least 10 h off between shifts, up to 7 consecutive shifts with a maximum of 56 working hours per week, and at least 24 h off between work sets. For sleep hours, the most common health-based recommendations were 7-9 h per 24-hour period and at least 5 h for safety-based recommendations. Importantly, many guidelines offered more stringent recommendations under conditions common in mining (i.e., early and night shifts). Several documents acknowledged needing to balance operational demands with efforts to mitigate fatigue risk, offering contingency-based strategies to help manage both. This synthesis gives mining safety practitioners context with which to influence schedule designs informed by industry-specific recommendations, while referencing other sectors with similar demands.

papers.title: Digital Device Use, Sleep Quality, and Well-Being Among Chinese Engineering Undergraduates.
papers.abstract: This study aimed to examine associations among total daily digital device use, sleep quality, and well-being in Chinese engineering undergraduates. It also sought to assess a contemporaneous indirect statistical association through sleep quality and to distinguish between-person differences from within-person deviations. Two survey waves conducted in June 2024 and December 2024 to January 2025 yielded 887 observations from 598 students, including 289 who participated at both waves. Students reported device-use duration, sleep quality, sleep duration, and well-being. Population-averaged generalized estimating equations, planned use-group contrasts, cluster-bootstrap path analysis, and Mundlak-type within-between decomposition adjusted for sociodemographic and academic covariates and survey wave. Reported device use of 6 h/day or more was associated with lower well-being (b=-0.192, 95% CI -0.322 to -0.062) and poorer sleep quality (b=0.127, 95% CI 0.019 to 0.236). Compared with 3 to <6 h/day, ≥6 h/day was associated with poorer outcomes, whereas differences for <3 h/day were not statistically significant. Sleep quality formed a small negative indirect statistical association between high use and well-being (ab=-0.045, bootstrap 95% CI -0.091 to -0.003). Significant associations were concentrated between persons; within-person deviations were not consistently associated with concurrent changes in sleep or well-being. The between-person findings suggest that high total device use may be a preliminary marker of students who also report poorer sleep and well-being. The ≥6-h/day category is not a validated threshold, and the findings do not show that reducing an individual student's use would improve these outcomes. Student support should consider digital-use patterns alongside sleep difficulties rather than impose uniform time limits.

papers.title: Efficacy of Stellate Ganglion Block Combined with Press-Needle Therapy in Patients with Insomnia Disorder of Heart-Spleen Deficiency Pattern: A Randomized Sham-Controlled Trial.
papers.abstract: Stellate ganglion block (SGB) may improve insomnia symptoms, and active press-needle therapy may enhance this effect. This study evaluated whether SGB combined with active press-needle therapy improves sleep quality in patients with insomnia disorder and a heart-spleen deficiency pattern. This single-center, randomized, sham-controlled trial enrolled and randomized 72 adults with insomnia disorder diagnosed according to the International Classification of Sleep Disorders, Third Edition (ICSD-3), Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) score ≥10, and heart-spleen deficiency pattern. Participants received ultrasound-guided SGB once daily for 10 days and were randomized to active or sham press-needle therapy. The primary outcome was change in PSQI score; secondary outcomes included Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9), Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7), serum cortisol, and wearable-recorded sleep parameters. After excluding 8 participants due to incomplete follow-up data, 64 participants (32 per group) were included in the final analysis. Post-treatment PSQI scores were lower with active than sham press-needle therapy: 12.00 (10.00, 14.00) vs 14.00 (11.00, 15.00), with a Hodges-Lehmann median difference of -2.00 points (95% CI, -3.00 to 0.00; Mann-Whitney U = 340.50; P = 0.020). At 2-week follow-up, PSQI scores were 9.00 (7.00, 12.00) vs 12.00 (10.00, 15.00), with a mean difference of -3.56 points (95% CI, -5.18 to -1.94; P < 0.001). PHQ-9 improvement was greater in the active group, whereas GAD-7 improvement did not differ significantly. Serum cortisol decreased in the active group but increased in the sham group. Wearable-recorded total sleep time showed a significant overall between-group effect, but the group-by-time interaction was not significant. No serious adverse events occurred. In adults with chronic insomnia receiving stellate ganglion block, adjunctive active press-needle therapy was associated with greater short-term improvement in subjective sleep quality than sham therapy. Effects on wearable-recorded sleep parameters were limited and require confirmation in larger trials using objective sleep assessment.

papers.title: A Tutorial on Automated Mass Spectral Analysis Using NucleoSpec for Compositional Assignment of Nucleic Acid-Silver Complexes and Nanoclusters.
papers.abstract: Nucleic acid-metal complexes, such as DNA-stabilized silver nanoclusters (DNA-Ag N ) and Ag-(I)-mediated DNA duplexes, show promise for applications ranging from biomedical imaging to bioelectronics and sensing. Electrospray ionization mass spectrometry (ESI-MS) is a powerful tool for precisely resolving their compositions, but the data analysis procedure can be challenging and time-consuming. No general-purpose software can automatically assign compositions of nucleic acid-silver complexes, most notably for DNA-Ag N , whose masses depend on the oxidation state of the silver core. We address these challenges by developing an automated data analysis workflow for ESI-MS of nucleic acid-silver complexes. This tutorial presents the analysis workflow and introduces NucleoSpec, an open-source, web-based platform that consolidates charge state determination, constraint-based composition enumeration, isotope-pattern matching, and adduct/conjugate handling into a single browser-accessible interface. The platform is benchmarked on published molecular formulas determined by manual analysis for DNA-Ag N , xeno-nucleic acid stabilized Ag N (XNA-Ag N ), nucleic acid-Ag-(I) complexes, and chemically modified DNA-Ag N , reproducing assignments to single-proton precision (median centroid offset of 0.03 m/z) for spectra of adequate signal-to-noise. Low-signal peaks for which adjacent valence electron counts become difficult to distinguish are flagged by NucleoSpec for user inspection. By lowering the barrier to high-resolution compositional analysis and supporting integration into high-throughput pipelines, NucleoSpec addresses a key experimental bottleneck in informatics-guided design of nucleic acid-metal complexes.

papers.title: Changes in sleep disturbances and quality of life associated with Istradefylline in patients with Parkinson's disease: an exploratory polysomnographic study.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances are common non-motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease (PD) and substantially impair quality of life (QOL). Although istradefylline, an adenosine A2A receptor antagonist, is widely used to improve motor fluctuations, its effects on subjective sleep complaints and objective sleep architecture remain unclear. In this exploratory, single-center, open-label study, we evaluated changes in subjective sleep quality and polysomnographic findings following 12 weeks of istradefylline treatment in patients with PD. Nine patients underwent clinical assessments and overnight polysomnography at baseline and 12 weeks after initiating istradefylline (20 mg/day). Sleep quality, QOL, fatigue, and motor symptoms were assessed using validated clinical scales. Following istradefylline initiation, improvements were observed in Parkinson's Disease Sleep Scale-2 (PDSS-2), Parkinson's Disease Questionnaire-39 summary index (PDQ-39 SI), Parkinson Fatigue Scale, and Movement Disorder Society-Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (MDS-UPDRS) Part IV scores. Changes in PDSS-2 scores were significantly correlated with changes in PDQ-39 SI (ρ = 0.76, p = 0.017), although both measures were subjective and obtained at the same assessment. Regarding objective sleep measures, most polysomnographic parameters did not significantly change; rapid eye movement (REM) sleep percentage increased numerically, but the change was not statistically significant (p = 0.058). In this small uncontrolled study, initiation of istradefylline was associated with improvements in subjective sleep quality, fatigue, and QOL, whereas objective polysomnographic parameters showed limited changes. These findings are exploratory and hypothesis-generating and require confirmation in larger controlled studies.

papers.title: Effect of epidural spinal cord stimulation combined with personalized neurorehabilitation in chronic motor-complete spinal cord injury: study protocol for the phase II single-arm feasibility RESTORES (RESToration Of Rehabilitative function with Epidural spinal Stimulation) trial.
papers.abstract: Chronic motor-complete spinal cord injury (SCI) results in profound neurological disability with minimal prospects for functional recovery using conventional rehabilitation strategies. Emerging evidence suggests that epidural spinal cord stimulation (eSCS) can activate dormant spinal locomotor networks and restore volitional and autonomic functions when combined with intensive activity-based training. However, systematic evaluation of multimodal neuromodulation approaches integrating advanced rehabilitation and computational neurophysiology remains limited. The RESTORES trial (RESToration Of Rehabilitative function with Epidural spinal Stimulation) is a prospective, single-arm Phase II feasibility study enrolling 15 adults with chronic (≥1 year) motor-complete SCI (American Spinal Injury Association Impairment scale (AIS) A or B) between C5 and T12. Participants will undergo implantation of an epidural spinal cord stimulator followed by a 24-week program of structured stimulation-coupled personalised neurorehabilitation (five sessions per week). Clinical outcomes will be evaluated using standardized neurological and functional measures including the AIS motor score, Spinal Cord Independence Measure version III (SCIM-III), Walking Index for Spinal Cord Injury II (WISCI-II), and Trunk Assessment Scale (TASS). Autonomic function and quality of life will also be assessed. Multimodal neurophysiological measurements-including surface electromyography (sEMG), electroencephalography (EEG), resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI), and computer-vision-based movement analysis-will be performed to investigate neural recovery mechanisms and inform the development of adaptive neuromodulation systems. The primary outcome is the safety of epidural spinal cord stimulation implantation, defined as the absence of device explantation for safety-related reasons within 6 months following implantation. Secondary outcomes include changes in AIS motor score, functional outcomes (SCIM, WISCI-II, TASS), autonomic function, quality of life, and neurophysiological biomarkers. This study integrates neuromodulation, advanced rehabilitation technologies, and multimodal computational neurophysiology to evaluate both clinical efficacy and neural mechanisms of recovery following chronic SCI. Findings from the RESTORES trial will provide critical safety and feasibility data to inform future multicenter trials and the development of closed-loop spinal cord stimulation systems. ClinicalTrials.gov, Identifier NCT05644171.

papers.title: Prevalence of Obstructive Sleep Apnea in the Adult Population of Saudi Arabia: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a common but often overlooked disorder with profound cardiometabolic and neurocognitive consequences. Various studies in Saudi Arabia have reported varying prevalence figures. To estimate the pooled prevalence of OSA among adults in Saudi Arabia. The systematic review and meta-analysis were carried out between May and August 2025 according to PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Observational studies that described the prevalence of OSA among adults (≥16 years) were considered. Pooled prevalence was computed using a random-effect model with Freeman-Tukey transformation. I2 statistics were used to determine the heterogeneity. Subgroup analysis was undertaken according to population, diagnostic tool, size of the sample, and region. Thirty-three studies with 18,403 participants were included. The overall pooled prevalence of OSA was 26.96% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 20.98%-33.38%), with high heterogeneity (I 2 = 98.9%). This significant heterogeneity is primarily attributed to variations in study populations (general vs. high-risk) and the diverse diagnostic criteria employed across the included studies. The prevalence was 15.95% (95% CI: 11.80%-20.60%) in the general population and 42.60% (95% CI: 29.47%-56.27%) in high-risk groups. The diagnostic method influenced estimates, with polysomnography (34.1%) and STOP-BANG (33.8%) yielding higher prevalence than the Berlin Questionnaire (28.5%). Regional variation was observed, with higher prevalence in Riyadh compared to Mecca. About one in four Saudi adults may have OSA, with prevalence markedly higher in high-risk groups. These findings underscore the need for national screening programs and targeted interventions to reduce the burden of undiagnosed OSA.

papers.title: Beyond Observable Behavior: A Narrative Review of Integrated Clinical, Biological, and Functional Assessment in Children With Autism Spectrum Disorder.
papers.abstract: Assessment of children with autism spectrum disorder must characterize everyday functioning, co-occurring conditions, and individual support needs alongside diagnostic classification. This narrative review examines the evidence and clinical rationale for integrated clinical, biological, and functional assessment in pediatric autism and presents SMART-NB as a proposed framework for organizing these dimensions. The review combines selected clinical guidelines and research publications with conceptual analysis and a targeted literature update, distinguishing established assessment principles from the author-developed framework. Three findings emerge. First, standardized observational instruments contribute to diagnosis but require interpretation alongside developmental history, caregiver information, differential diagnosis, and clinical judgment. Second, co-occurring sleep disturbances, gastrointestinal symptoms, nutritional problems, sensory impairments, and pain can influence behavior and participation and warrant clinically directed evaluation; their association with autism does not establish causation. Third, symptom severity does not fully describe adaptive functioning, supporting assessment across functional domains and everyday contexts. SMART-NB proposes connecting clinical, medical and biological, and demand-related profiles with seven functional domains, individualized goals, and longitudinal reassessment. The demand dimension examines available capacity, physiological and emotional burden, environmental requirements, and supports. Its proposed contribution is to document how assessment findings inform care priorities. Existing multidimensional approaches already address overlapping aspects of this task; the incremental value of this particular organization remains untested. The reviewed evidence supports multidimensional assessment but does not establish the validity, reliability, or clinical utility of SMART-NB. This review is not systematic, and extension beyond autism remains a hypothesis requiring condition-specific evaluation. Development should proceed from operational specification, independent content assessment, and feasibility studies to the evaluation of measurement properties and comparative clinical outcomes.

papers.title: Occupational Therapy Interventions Addressing Activities of Daily Living and Sleep for People With Multiple Sclerosis: A Systematic Review.
papers.abstract: The effectiveness of occupational therapy (OT) services for people with multiple sclerosis (MS) has not been updated since the last systematic review in 2010, particularly outcomes within the scope of OT practice. The objective of this systematic review was to appraise evidence published since 2011 on the effectiveness of interventions within the scope of OT practice for activities of daily living (ADL) and sleep in adults with MS. Quantitative studies (Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine Levels of Evidence 1b through 3b) from January 2011 through July 2023 were systematically reviewed through 3 literature searches performed in January 2019, February 2022, and July 2023 using the Medline, APA PsycInfo, Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature, OTseeker, and Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. Inclusion criteria were adult participants with MS and OT-related interventions that addressed ADL or sleep. All authors independently screened titles and abstracts and then appraised full-text articles. Then at least 2 authors analyzed and grouped included articles into outcomes of interest. Risk of bias for study quality and strength of evidence were then analyzed. The review included 45 studies on sleep, falls and functional mobility, toileting hygiene (continence), sexual activity, and general ADL. Cognitive behavioral therapy, mindfulness training, targeted exercise programs, and counseling using the Permission, Limited Information, Specific Suggestions, and Intensive Therapy model or the Good Enough Sex model were effective in adults with MS. Occupational therapists can provide interventions using the above approaches, which have been shown to empirically improve ADL function and sleep outcomes. Researchers, consumers, and practitioners should consider demographic and diagnostic differences when generalizing these findings.

papers.title: Spontaneous reduction of a posteriorly dislocated mobile-bearing insert in a medial unicompartmental knee replacement: A case report.
papers.abstract: Posterior dislocation of the mobile polyethylene bearing is an uncommon complication of medial Unicompartmental Knee Replacement (UKR) that is diagnosed radiographically and typically requires manipulation under anaesthesia or revision surgery. We report a 67-year-old man with a 7-year history of bilateral medial UKR who presented with a locked, painful knee at 60° of flexion after a twisting injury. Radiographs demonstrated posterior dislocation of the bearing, with collapse of the medial joint space and metal-on-metal contact between the femoral and tibial components. The 3 radiopaque metallic markers in the polyethylene bearing helped to visualise the location of the bearing behind the medial femoral condyle. While the patient awaited manipulation under anaesthesia, spontaneous relocation occurred overnight during sleep in a lateral position. Repeat radiographs on the following morning confirmed anatomical reduction of the meniscus bearing, with clinical resolution of symptoms. Awareness of this radiographic pattern, and of its potential for spontaneous resolution, can help radiologists and referring orthopaedic clinicians avoid unnecessary further investigations and urgent surgical intervention.

papers.title: Patient-Performed Neck Encirclement Within the NoSAS Score: Score Availability and Diagnostic Performance in a Tertiary Sleep Centre.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is highly prevalent, and early identification remains a major public health challenge. The NoSAS score is a simple and validated screening tool, incorporating neck circumference >40 cm. However, neck circumference measurement may be inconsistently performed in routine practice. Patient-performed neck encirclement, an equipment-free hand-based maneuver, may represent a pragmatic alternative. We conducted a retrospective analysis of prospectively collected routine clinical data including 449 consecutive patients referred for suspected OSA in a tertiary sleep center (Lyon, France) between September and December 2025. Neck circumference and Patient-performed manual neck encirclement were assessed at the same anatomical level. Diagnostic performance was evaluated for apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) thresholds ≥15 and ≥30 events·h-1. A modified NoSAS score incorporating patient-performed neck encirclement (NoSAS hand) was compared with the standard score. In paired complete-case comparisons, diagnostic estimates and between-score differences were reported with 95% confidence intervals and McNemar tests. Patient-performed neck encirclement was substantially more available than measured neck circumference (94.0% vs 71.3%) and NoSAS hand was calculable more often than standard NoSAS (91.3% vs 68.8%). In the paired complete-case cohort (n=305), at AHI ≥15/h, sensitivity and specificity differences (NoSAS hand minus standard NoSAS) were 0.0% (95% CI -1.9 to 1.9) and +1.0% (95% CI -2.0 to 5.1), respectively; corresponding differences at AHI ≥30/h were 0.0% (95% CI -2.5 to 2.5) and +0.5% (95% CI -1.6 to 2.7). Patient-performed neck encirclement is a simple, equipment-free alternative to measured neck circumference that substantially improves the feasibility of NoSAS implementation while preserving diagnostic performance. In this tertiary sleep-centre workflow, patient-performed neck encirclement was recorded more often than measured neck circumference and increased NoSAS score availability; paired point estimates of sensitivity and specificity at AHI ≥15/h and ≥30/h differed little between scores.

papers.title: Chronotype and Emotion-Regulation as Determinants of Bedtime Procrastination in Adolescents: The Mediating Role of Sleep Hygiene Practices.
papers.abstract: The current study investigates whether sleep hygiene patterns mediate the relationship between chronotype, emotion-regulation, and bedtime procrastination among adolescents. The study hypothesizes that adolescents with evening type and lower emotion regulation will exhibit more bedtime procrastination, and that this relationship will be mediated by poor sleep hygiene. Utilizing a cross-sectional design, 486 students from secondary schools in Slovakia completed questionnaires assessing sleep patterns and behavior, circadian preference and difficulties in regulation of emotions. Data were analyzed using simple mediation model with bootstrapping to assess the associations of the variables with bedtime procrastination directly and indirectly through sleep hygiene as mediator. The results showed that bedtime procrastination exhibited a positive and statistically significant relationship with emotion-regulation difficulties and statistically significant negative relationship with chronotype and sleep hygiene. Furthermore, chronotype displayed a negative and statistically significant association with emotion-regulation difficulties. Mediation analysis revealed that both emotion regulation difficulties and chronotype showed direct and indirect associations with bedtime procrastination through sleep hygiene. However, the indirect association was stronger for emotion regulation difficulties, whereas association between chronotype and bedtime procrastination was primarily direct. The final model explained 35.6% of the variance in bedtime procrastination (R2 =0.356). The present study highlights the associations underlying bedtime procrastination from both self-regulatory and circadian perspectives, with sleep hygiene emerging as a significant variable associated with relationship between individual predispositions and bedtime procrastination. Interventions focusing on enhancing self-regulation capacities could be relevant for improving bedtime routines, hygiene and consequent behavior.

papers.title: Tegmental atrophy in isolated REM sleep behaviour disorder: ex vivo MRI-informed in vivo imaging.
papers.abstract: Isolated rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behaviour disorder (iRBD) is an early-stage synucleinopathy characterized by brainstem pathology. In rodents, the pontine tegmentum contains a REM sleep centre, the sublaterodorsal nucleus, which expresses corticotropin-releasing hormone binding protein (CRHBP). While the involvement of brainstem pathophysiology is thus implicated in iRBD, its solid evidence remains scarce in humans due to the difficulty in identifying small brainstem nuclei with conventional MRI technology alone. Here, we aimed to detect tegmental atrophy in iRBD with voxel-based morphometry (VBM) analysis combined with a novel human brainstem atlas. Structural MRIs from 98 patients with iRBD and 114 controls were analysed to investigate grey matter volume using VBM. Our unique approach involved detailed assessments of the VBM results, guided by a high-resolution MRI-based atlas of the human brainstem. This brainstem atlas was founded on ex vivo MRI of 10 post-mortem human specimens. We validated it with CRHBP immunostaining, which aided in identifying putative REM sleep-regulating nuclei in humans. We applied this brainstem atlas to identify atrophy in specific brainstem regions in iRBD and correlate their volumes with clinical and polysomnographic measures. Voxel-based morphometry revealed a focal cluster of grey matter atrophy in the dorsal pontine tegmentum of iRBD patients, including the laterodorsal tegmental nucleus, ventral part (LDTgV) and the pedunculopontine tegmental nucleus (PTg). Our atlas-based analysis confirmed the LDTgV as the site of most conspicuous atrophy, revealing a significant volume reduction in iRBD patients compared with controls with a moderate effect size (Cohen's d = 0.44, Bonferroni-corrected P = 0.019). Furthermore, greater atrophy in the LDTgV and the PTg was associated with more severe autonomic dysfunction as measured by Scales for Outcomes in Parkinson's Disease-Autonomic dysfunction scores (partial r = -0.237, P = 0.021 and partial r = -0.236, P = 0.021, respectively). In 23 patients from whom quantitative polysomnographic data were available, LDTgV atrophy was correlated with the percentage ratio of REM sleep without atonia (partial r = -0.491, P = 0.028). Histological analysis confirmed that the LDTgV is selectively enriched with CRHBP-positive neurons, a putative marker for REM sleep-on neurons. We provided novel evidence for the involvement of LDTgV, the putative human homologue of the murine sublaterodorsal nucleus, in iRBD. The present findings advance our understanding of the neuroanatomical basis of iRBD and will contribute to the development of early biomarkers for α-synucleinopathies.

papers.title: Beyond the light-driven pacemaker: the suprachiasmatic nucleus as a dynamic coordinator of environmental cues.
papers.abstract: The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) is the central mammalian circadian pacemaker, but its function extends beyond passive entrainment to light. Here, we synthesize evidence that the SCN is a heterogeneous and plastic network that integrates photic, metabolic, astrocytic, and thermal information across daily entrainment, seasonal adaptation, jet lag, and chronic circadian misalignment. VIP and GRP neurons provide privileged access for retinal input and network synchronization, AVP neurons support intrinsic rhythmicity and output, and the broad Nms-expressing ensemble and CCK-defined subtypes contribute to arousal and adaptive network plasticity. We propose an integrative circuit model in which retinal signals preferentially engage core VIP/GRP neurons, whereas feeding and metabolic information influences VIP and AVP populations through circulating factors, the dorsomedial hypothalamus, the intergeniculate leaflet, and metabolically responsive astrocytes. Rhythmic astrocytic GABA and glutamate release, together with VIP-AVP coupling and overlapping VIP+/NMS+ and AVP+/NMS+ subpopulations, may coordinate phase resetting and sleep-wake rhythms. The timing mechanism underlying food anticipatory activity (FAA) is attributed primarily to distributed extra-SCN food-entrainable circuits, whereas the SCN may gate or modulate its behavioral expression rather than generate it autonomously. Light remains the dominant zeitgeber. Under standard light-dark conditions, time-restricted feeding more commonly modulates SCN neuronal activity, calcium dynamics, neuropeptide output, and behavior than resets the core TTFL; molecular resetting has been reported only under specific genetic, temporal, dietary, lighting, or network conditions. When light and feeding cues conflict, rapid ventral resetting and slower dorsal reentrainment generate transient intranuclear and systemic desynchrony rather than simple dominance by either cue. Biological sex and aging further shape this integrative capacity, while temperature compensation delineates the boundary between resistance to routine thermal fluctuations and conditional responses to stronger thermal challenges. This framework helps explain circadian disruption in jet lag, shift work, social jetlag, and metabolic disease, and supports circadian medicine strategies that align timed light, feeding, exercise, sleep, and pharmacotherapy across central and peripheral clocks.

papers.title: Vestibular dysfunction in patients with obstructive sleep apnea: from physiopathology to treatment.
papers.abstract: Sleep disorders include a wide variety of conditions that can have serious consequences on general health. The most common sleep problem related to breathing is obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). The Ear, Nose, and Throat (ENT) manifestations of this pathology are numerous including balance disorders. Understanding the impact of OSA on the vestibular function in Meniere's disease, vestibular migraine, and benign paroxysmal positional vertigo ensure a systematic screening and an appropriate care.

papers.title: Longitudinal Associations Between Depressive Symptoms and Brain Structure Across Late Childhood and Adolescence: A Panel Network Analysis Study.
papers.abstract: Major depressive disorder is the leading cause of nonfatal disability in youth and disproportionately affects adolescent females. Structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) studies of adolescent depression have yielded inconsistent findings, potentially reflecting symptom heterogeneity and rapid developmental changes in brain morphology. We examined associations between specific depressive symptoms and structural brain MRI measures in 9761 youth (53.1% male, ages 8.32-18.0 years) from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study across 4 waves. A panel graphical vector autoregression model separated within-person (contemporaneous and temporal) effects from between-person effects. Brain measures included cortical thickness in 4 regions, hippocampal volume, and global surface area. Depressive symptoms included parent-reported depressed mood, anhedonia, lethargy, worthlessness, and sleep problems. Sex differences in network structure were also examined. Strong within-domain associations were observed among brain measures and symptoms. Cross-domain associations emerged at both within-person and between-person levels. Within persons, higher depressed mood predicted subsequent decreases in global surface area, whereas higher worthlessness predicted subsequent increases; depressed mood was also linked to medial orbitofrontal cortex thickness over time and to lower global surface area concurrently. At the between-person level, individuals with higher average anhedonia showed lower average global surface area. Sex differences were confined to the within-person networks. Brain-symptom associations were subtle, symptom specific, and present across network levels with differential edge stability. Global surface area emerged as the primary structural correlate. Longitudinal within-person approaches capture the coupling of within-person deviations from expected brain and symptom trajectories, complementing between-person approaches in understanding brain-depression co-fluctuation during adolescence.

papers.title: Negative regulation of TH17-mediated inflammation by the nuclear receptor REV-ERBβ.
papers.abstract: TH17 cells play a central role in several human autoimmune diseases. We and others reported the nuclear receptor, REV-ERBα, as a cell-intrinsic repressor of TH17-mediated pathogenicity. REV-ERBβ, REV-ERBα's closely related family member, is thought to be functionally redundant to REV-ERBα, which we sought to explore in TH17-mediated immunity. Our data indicate that deletion of REV-ERBβ enhances TH17-mediated pro-inflammatory cytokine expression and exacerbated disease in mouse models of multiple sclerosis and colitis. RNA-sequencing indicates REV-ERBβ and REV-ERBα do not have similar transcriptional profiles in TH17 cells. REV-ERBβ does not appear to strongly rely on interaction with the classic co-repressor NCoR1 to regulate gene expression, which is in contrast to REV-ERBα in TH17 cells, nor does it utilize heme, its known endogenous ligand for its repressive functions. Our results establish that while REV-ERBβ also acts as a negative regulator of TH17-cell function and pathogenicity, it does so in a manner that is non-redundant, independent, and unique to REV-ERBα.

papers.title: Modifiable glymphatic-related brain clearance physiology in humans: a critical narrative review of interventional evidence.
papers.abstract: The glymphatic model proposes that cerebrospinal fluid exchanges with interstitial fluid along perivascular pathways, potentially facilitating brain solute clearance. Interest in whether this physiology can be modified has prompted human studies of sleep, exercise, respiratory manipulation, circadian interventions, and neuromodulation, but these studies use endpoints that differ substantially in biological directness. This critical narrative review evaluates human interventional and longitudinal evidence for modifiable glymphatic-related brain-clearance physiology and distinguishes altered neurofluid dynamics from evidence of solute transport. Sleep provides the most convincing convergent evidence: total sleep deprivation impairs intrathecal tracer clearance, whereas normal sleep increases the overnight appearance of amyloid-β and tau in plasma. Sustained aerobic exercise modifies contrast-based brain influx and meningeal lymphatic measures, although evidence remains preliminary. Slow deep breathing and intermittent hypercapnia alter cerebrospinal fluid dynamics; hypercapnia also increases several plasma brain-protein concentrations, but enhanced clearance is unconfirmed. Bright light therapy and transcranial magnetic stimulation modify diffusion-based perivascular imaging proxies that remain indirect and biologically nonspecific. Human neurofluid physiology may therefore be modifiable, but changes in fluid motion or surrogate imaging signals should not be equated with enhanced solute clearance. Clinically meaningful modulation will require controlled studies linking mechanistic target engagement to direct solute transport and neurological outcomes.
