papers.title: Distinct electrophysiological correlates of low- and high-level visual consciousness with minimized post-perceptual processing.
papers.abstract: Conscious visual phenomenology comprises multiple representational levels, from basic features to integrated percepts, raising the question of how the neural correlates of consciousness (NCC) differentiate accordingly. Event-related potential (ERP) studies identified early occipitotemporal negativities as reliable NCC; yet, it remains unclear whether these capture conscious content beyond low-level features and extend to higher-order representations. Moreover, whether later ERP components index higher-level conscious percepts independent of task-related processing remains contested. The present study addresses this question using an inattentional blindness (IB) paradigm that isolates three representational levels of conscious perception (no, low- or high-level awareness) for an identical stimulus under minimized post-perceptual processing. Across 85 healthy participants, low-level line perception was indexed by an enhanced early occipital negativity, whereas high-level face perception additionally recruited a right-lateralized occipitotemporal negativity, followed by medial posterior positivities. These findings reveal systematic spatiotemporal differentiation of awareness-related potentials across representational levels of consciousness under task-irrelevant conditions.

papers.title: Effect of a Researcher-Supervised Walking Program With Smartphone-Based Step Monitoring on Sleep Quality in Older Psychiatric Inpatients: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
papers.abstract: Sleep disorders are common among hospitalized older adults with psychiatric conditions and may adversely affect health. Structured walking is a promising nonpharmacological intervention, and smartphone-based step monitoring may support adherence. This study evaluated the effect of a researcher-supervised walking program supported by smartphone-based step monitoring on sleep quality in older adults admitted to a psychiatric hospital in Guilan Province, Iran. In this randomized controlled trial, 62 hospitalized older adults were randomly assigned to the intervention or control groups. The intervention group received routine care plus a 4-week researcher-supervised walking program supported by smartphone-based step monitoring, consisting of 30-min outdoor walking sessions three times weekly. The control group received routine care alone. Sleep quality was assessed using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) at baseline and postintervention. The primary outcome was global PSQI score, assessed at baseline and postintervention. The prespecified primary analysis was ANCOVA; because its assumptions were not fully met, a post hoc change score analysis was conducted using Welch's t-test. Cohen's d with 95% confidence intervals was reported. Complete outcome data were available for 55 of the 62 randomized participants, and the primary analysis used a complete case approach without imputation. The mean PSQI score decreased from 12.93 ± 3.94 to 5.89 ± 3.48 in the intervention group and from 11.64 ± 3.94 to 9.39 ± 3.07 in the control group. The intervention group demonstrated significantly greater improvement in PSQI scores (between-group mean difference in change: -4.79, 95% CI -6.05 to -3.52; Cohen's d = 2.09, 95% CI 1.44-2.77). A researcher-supervised walking program supported by smartphone-based step monitoring was associated with improved sleep quality in hospitalized older adults with psychiatric disorders and may be a feasible non-pharmacological adjunct to routine inpatient care.

papers.title: Student outcomes in a student-led clinic: beyond clinical learning.
papers.abstract: Student-assisted, -run or -led health clinics (SLCs) are increasingly common worldwide, but student outcomes remain under-evaluated, with existing work focused narrowly on clinical and/or academic outcomes. This study presents the findings of an evaluation of the impact of a student-assisted clinic in New Zealand, on participating students subjective wellbeing, assessed using the Satisfaction with Life Scale (SWLS), as well as on a range of programme-related intermediate outcomes theorised to support wellbeing, including leadership, communication, and clinical capability. Students undertaking placements at the clinic were surveyed at three time points: at the start, the end, and at six months post-placement. Participating students maintained levels of self-reported wellbeing over placement periods while significantly improving leadership, purpose, cultural connection, and clinical capability. Income and sleep were shown to be key factors related to SWLS scores. Student-related outcomes from SLCs may extend beyond clinical care and academic performance, highlighting the value of a more holistic approach to SLC evaluation.

papers.title: Case Report: An MDT-guided multimodal protocol for large-area stroke plateau - integrating neuromodulation with multimodal assessment.
papers.abstract: This case report investigates the feasibility and potential value of an individualized precision rehabilitation protocol for large-area stroke, integrating multimodal neuromodulation under the guidance of a multidisciplinary team (MDT) and dynamic assessment. A 38-year-old male with right hemiplegia and global aphasia following large left hemispheric infarction underwent an 8-month MDT-managed program. A closed-loop "assess-decide-intervene-re-assess" framework was implemented, featuring periodic multimodal evaluations (clinical scales, DTI, fMRI, EEG, 3D gait analysis). The intervention dynamically combined conventional therapy with staged neuromodulation: repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (rTMS) for aphasia and intermittent Theta Burst Stimulation (iTBS) for motor disorder, Brain-Computer Interface (BCI)-robotic training and task-oriented Virtual Reality (VR) for upper limb function, and biomechanical correction with custom insoles based on gait analysis. Notable functional improvements were observed: LOTCA increased by 16 points, CRRCAE subscale improved by 60%-90%, FMA increased from 20 to 56, FMA-B reached 12, and MBI improved from 40 to 91. Neuroimaging revealed increased fractional anisotropy (FA) in the corpus callosum and right corticospinal tract, and elevated ALFF/ReHo in right frontal-temporal areas. Event-related desynchronization (ERD) decreased during BCI training, and gait parameters improved. In this patient with large-area stroke who showed limited response to conventional rehabilitation, an MDT-guided, dynamically adjusted multimodal intervention was temporally associated with concurrent recovery across cognitive, language, motor, and daily living domains. The concomitant neural changes suggest possible trans-hemispheric network reorganization. These observations are hypothesis-generating and, while limited by the single-case design, provide a preliminary rationale for future investigations into precision neurorehabilitation approaches in similar complex cases. ChiCTR2300069203.

papers.title: Time-varying associations of temperature and sleep as a marker of heat adaptation: A case study of Spanish outdoor workers over one summer of continuous monitoring.
papers.abstract: Rising global temperatures are increasingly recognized as a threat to sleep health. Outdoor workers, who often endure prolonged exposure to outdoor heat, may also be impacted by indoor nighttime temperatures. However, few studies have examined both exposures in this population, and, little is known about potential adaptation to heat in relation to sleep outcomes. We conducted an intensive longitudinal study with 13 Spanish outdoor workers over a 3-month summer period, during which sleep outcomes (i.e., total sleep time [TST], sleep efficiency [SE], and subjective sleep quality) were measured daily via an activity monitor and ecological momentary assessments. Temperatures were monitored both indoors and outdoors, using bedroom sensors and weather station data. Linear mixed-effects models were used to quantify the daily associations between heat and sleep. Across the whole summer, each 1 °C increase in outdoor and indoor temperature led respectively to decreases of 2.13 (95% CI: -3.84, -0.42) and 3.18 (95% CI: -5.67, -0.70) minutes in total sleep time (TST); 0.09 (95% CI: -0.17, -0.01) and 0.18 (95% CI: -0.30, -0.07) percentage points in sleep efficiency (SE); and 0.09 (95% CI: -0.14, -0.04) and 0.17 (95% CI: -0.24, -0.09) points in subjective sleep quality. Time-varying analyses revealed that the adverse effects of heat on subjective sleep quality were attenuated in August compared with June and July for similar temperatures. We found that both indoor and outdoor temperatures were associated with poorer sleep outcomes during the whole summer, along with preliminary evidence of reduced heat-related effects on subjective sleep quality later in the summer.
papers.journal: The journal of climate change and health

papers.title: A SynNotch-PiggyBac gene circuit for inflammation-responsive IL-10 delivery in Alzheimer's disease: a hypothesis and design framework.
papers.abstract: Chronic neuroinflammation driven by sustained microglial and astrocyte activation contributes to Alzheimer's disease progression, yet no therapeutic strategy addresses it with precision or durability in the brain. Interleukin-10 occupies an unresolved position in this problem. Constitutive interleukin-10 overexpression in amyloid precursor protein transgenic mice increased plaque burden by suppressing microglial phagocytic activity, while interleukin-10 deletion has been reported to restrict amyloidosis in one setting and to worsen tau hyperphosphorylation in another. We interpret this pattern as evidence that interleukin-10 carries opposite signs on the two principal pathologies of Alzheimer's disease, so that any therapy holding it at a fixed concentration is committed in advance to being wrong about one of them. We therefore propose a falsifiable hypothesis: conditional, inflammation-gated interleukin-10 expression may suppress damaging inflammatory signaling while limiting the impairment of microglial phagocytosis associated with continuous exposure. We present a design framework for a synthetic gene circuit combining an adeno-associated viral vector for delivery to the central nervous system, a synthetic Notch receptor that detects membrane-bound tumor necrosis factor alpha on activated microglia through juxtacrine contact, and a PiggyBac transposon intended to integrate the circuit into the astrocyte genome. Receptor engagement is expected to release a transcription factor that drives interleukin-10 from a synthetic promoter, with transcription ceasing as the stimulus is withdrawn. We provide a quantitative packaging analysis showing that the circuit requires a compacted vector design to fit within viral capacity, and we identify three unvalidated assumptions: the recognition domain does not yet exist, ligand surface density on activated microglia is unmeasured, and shed soluble tumor necrosis factor alpha is predicted to act as a competitive inhibitor of receptor activation. A computational analysis of simulated resting-state electroencephalography, in which 45 of 171 electrode pairs differed after false discovery rate correction, is presented as a fully specified analysis workflow for delta-band connectivity as a secondary outcome measure rather than as evidence of effect, and yields effect sizes indicating that a rodent study would need roughly 11 animals per group. A four-arm validation plan is specified that separates the contribution of conditional regulation from that of genomic integration.

papers.title: Health-risk behaviours among university students in Bulawayo, Zimbabwe.
papers.abstract: University students frequently engage in health-risk behaviours that may affect academic engagement, wellbeing, and campus experiences. Quantitative studies dominate the literature, leaving limited qualitative insight into how students in specific African university settings understand these behaviours and the contexts in which they occur. A single-site descriptive qualitative case study was conducted at a university in Bulawayo, Zimbabwe. Fifteen students aged 19-25 years participated in semi-structured telephone interviews. Five institutional documents provided supplementary contextual information. Data were analysed thematically using QDA Miner Lite and interpreted through a socio-ecological lens. Students described six interconnected health-risk behaviours: substance use, smoking and waterpipe use, risky sexual behaviours, physical inactivity, unhealthy dietary behaviours cancel practices, and inadequate and irregular sleep. These behaviours were understood as shaped by interacting peer, academic, financial, psychological, and institutional influences rather than as isolated individual choices. Some accounts reflected personal experiences, while others concerned behaviours observed among peers. Perceived consequences include difficulties with concentration and attendance, emotional wellbeing, physical wellbeing, and social relationships. Participants advocated accessible counselling, peer education, health information, healthier coping strategies, and student-informed institutional support. Health-risk behaviours among these students were embedded in interconnected personal, social, economic, academic, and institutional contexts. The findings highlight the importance of multi-level, student-informed approaches to university health promotion that address both individual coping and the broader conditions shaping health behaviours. Further multi-site qualitative and mixed-methods research is needed across diverse Zimbabwean and Southern African university settings.

papers.title: Editorial: Brain-based mechanisms underlying the cognitive, sleep, and emotional benefits of aerobic exercise.
Caregiver-reported oral health-related quality of life in children with Mowat-Wilson syndrome: a comparative study.
papers.abstract: Mowat-Wilson syndrome (MWS) is a rare genetic disorder characterized by intellectual disability, distinctive craniofacial features, behavioral impairments, and congenital anomalies. Although oral and craniofacial abnormalities are frequently reported, their impact on oral health-related quality of life (OHRQoL) has not been investigated. This study aimed to evaluate OHRQoL in children with MWS and compare it with peers with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and neurotypical controls. Secondary analyses explored caregiver functional limitations and dental care characteristics. A cross-sectional questionnaire-based study was conducted involving caregivers of children aged 6-18 years with MWS (n = 19), ASD (n = 19), and neurotypical controls (n = 38). OHRQoL was assessed using the short-form Parental-Caregiver Perception Questionnaire (P-CPQ) and Family Impact Scale (FIS). Additional questions explored socioeconomic characteristics, dental care setting and attendance, and parental perceptions of oral health. Group comparisons were performed using non-parametric and parametric tests, with significance set at p < 0.05. Children with MWS showed significantly higher total P-CPQ scores than neurotypical controls (37.11 ± 8.65 vs. 26.23 ± 5.05; p < 0.001), indicating poorer OHRQoL. The greatest impairments were observed in the functional limitation domain, particularly regarding chewing difficulties, mouth breathing, slower eating, and sleep disturbances (all p < 0.001). Halitosis and food impaction on the palate were also significantly more frequent in the MWS group. Parents of children with MWS reported a greater impact of oral conditions on wellbeing than both ASD and neurotypical groups (p < 0.05). Although OHRQoL impairment was comparable between MWS and ASD participants, ASD was associated with greater family burden, reflected by higher FIS scores (16.42 ± 7.09 vs. 21.58 ± 4.85; p = 0.016). Both MWS and ASD groups exhibited higher combined P-CPQ + FIS scores than neurotypical controls (p < 0.01). Both MWS and ASD were associated with poorer OHRQoL than neurotypical status, although distinct patterns of impairment emerged. MWS was primarily characterized by functional oral limitations and a greater impact of oral conditions on wellbeing, whereas ASD was associated with greater psychosocial and family burden. These findings support the existence of a syndrome-specific profile of caregiver-perceived unmet oral health needs and functional limitations in children with complex healthcare conditions and emphasize the importance of individualized, multidisciplinary dental care strategies.

papers.title: Patient counseling across neurologic subspecialties-a single academic center study.
papers.abstract: Counseling is a routine part of neurologic care, but little is known about how commonly it is documented. We sought to characterize counseling in routine neurologic care by determining the proportion of visits with documented counseling, describe forms of counseling, and investigate factors that predict documentation of counseling. We performed a cross-sectional study via retrospective chart reviews of 994 neurologic subspeciality outpatient encounters at a tertiary academic medical center from September 2023 to October 2023. The main outcome of this analysis was documented counseling (Yes/No) which was established via protocol-driven pre-specified chart review with assessment of abstraction reliability. Secondary outcomes included lifestyle modification (e.g., exercise, sleep, diet, alcohol, safety) and medication/disease specific education counseling (e.g., headache, seizure, medication, cognitive, stroke). We used a multivariable generalized estimating equations regression model with clustering at the provider level to compare how patient counseling varied across provider subspecialities. Out of 994 outpatient encounters, 38% (n = 374) of visits had any documented counseling. Counseling on medication/disease specific education (28%, n = 276) was more common than on lifestyle education (6%, n = 60). The neurologic subspecialties with highest percentage of documented counseling were headache (73%), epilepsy (51%), and stroke (41%) while the neurologic subspecialties with the lowest percentage of any documented patient counseling were neuromuscular (19%), cognitive (15%), and multiple sclerosis (11%). Headache subspecialists were the only provider group to have increased odds of counseling (OR = 3.6, CI: 1.3-9.9) compared to general neurologists, while cognitive and multiple sclerosis subspecialists had 73% (CI: 42%-78%) and 72% (CI: 25%-89%) lower odds of documenting any counseling. Patient demographics were not statistically significantly associated with frequency of counseling. Our study demonstrated significant variability in frequency and types of counseling documented across neurologic outpatient encounters and between subspecialists. The findings suggest that patient counseling may be undocumented and/or under-employed in certain fields. Future multi-centered studies are needed to understand documentation practices, actual performance of counseling relative to documentation, and patient clinical outcomes after participating in counseling.

papers.title: A robust adversarial learning framework for EEG emotion recognition.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) provides an objective means of capturing neural patterns associated with emotion, but substantial inter-subject variability limits the ability of existing models to generalize to unseen subjects. We propose a robust adversarial domain generalization framework for cross-subject EEG emotion recognition. In the first stage, long short-term memory-based encoders are jointly trained to learn domain-invariant and domain-specific representations using reconstruction, emotion classification, and adversarial domain objectives. This process preserves emotion-relevant information while suppressing subject-specific distribution shifts. In the second stage, the invariant encoder and emotion classifier are further refined through distributionally robust optimization with gradient-guided feature augmentation. Theframework is evaluated on the AMIGOS and DREAMER datasets using leave-one-subject-out cross-validation. The proposed method achieves mean accuracies of 69.94% and 68.97% and F1 scores of 0.59 and 0.65 on AMIGOS and DREAMER, respectively, outperforming the comparison methods on both datasets. Ablation results further show that adversarial learning provides the primary improvement in cross-subject generalization, while distributionally robust optimization offers complementary robustness. These findings indicate that combining representation learning that is invariant across domains with distributionally robust optimization effectively reduces distribution shifts across subjects and improves EEG emotion recognition for unseen subjects.

papers.title: Polysomnographic and nocturnal heart rate correlates of cognitive impairment in Parkinson's disease: a cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: To investigate the correlations between cognitive impairment in Parkinson's disease (PD) and nocturnal video-polysomnography (vPSG) and electrocardiogram (ECG) parameters, evaluating their independent clinical value. We analyzed 84 PD patients divided into normal cognition (PD-NC, n = 27), mild cognitive impairment (PD-MCI, n = 27), and dementia (PDD, n = 30) groups. Clinical scales, overnight vPSG, and electrocardiogram parameters were recorded. Multivariable linear regression was used to evaluate independent factors associated with the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) scores. As cognitive impairment progressed, REM sleep latency significantly shortened (128.82 ± 117.32 min in PDD vs. 200.54 ± 90.26 min in PD-NC, p = 0.006). Concurrently, mean nocturnal heart rate (65.80 ± 10.80 bpm) and minimum heart rate (50.77 ± 12.51 bpm) were significantly higher in the PDD group than in the other two groups (p < 0.01). Multivariable linear regression revealed that, after adjusting for age, education, and UPDRS III score, mean nocturnal heart rate remained independently and negatively associated with MoCA scores (B = -0.158, β = -0.264, t = -3.018, p = 0.003), while REM sleep latency was independently and positively associated with MoCA scores (B = 0.010, β = 0.192, t = 2.224, p = 0.029). Collinearity diagnostics showed no significant multicollinearity (VIF: 1.029-1.261). Higher mean nocturnal heart rate and shorter REM sleep latency were independently associated with lower global cognitive performance in PD patients. Both measures can be obtained from routine overnight PSG, although their physiological significance remains uncertain. The cross-sectional design and the absence of direct autonomic or cholinergic measurements preclude causal or mechanistic conclusions.

papers.title: Development and external validation of an explainable machine learning model for identifying depressive symptoms in middle-aged and older adults with low haemoglobin: a prediction-model study.
papers.abstract: Early screening for depressive symptoms in middle-aged and older adults is important for timely risk identification. Low haemoglobin may identify a clinically accessible vulnerable subgroup in which chronic disease burden, fatigue, functional impairment, and reduced physiological reserve often coexist. However, it should be understood as a high-risk phenotype rather than a direct measure of nutritional deficiency or frailty. Evidence in this population remains limited. This study developed a model using data from the 2015 China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS), with CHARLS 2011 and a cross-sectional cohort from Gansu Provincial People's Hospital used for temporal and external validation, respectively. Depressive symptoms were defined as a 10-item Centre for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale score ≥10. Candidate variables included sociodemographic, behavioural, health status, functional, cognitive, and comorbidity-related information. After least absolute shrinkage and selection operator feature selection, 16 variables were retained. Seven machine learning models were compared, and Random Forest was retained for interpretation and online tool development based on its balanced performance and interpretability. A total of 2,022 participants were included in the development cohort, 1,095 in the temporal validation cohort, and 400 in the external validation cohort. The AUROC values of the Random Forest model were 0.791, 0.776, and 0.809, respectively, with Brier scores of 0.182, 0.193, and 0.182, indicating stable discrimination and acceptable calibration. Shapley additive explanations analysis showed that sleep time, instrumental activities of daily living score, and activities of daily living score were the most important contributors. Threshold sensitivity analysis showed that lower probability thresholds increased sensitivity/recall but reduced specificity. A prototype online assessment tool was developed for individualised estimation of depressive symptom probability. This study developed and validated an interpretable machine learning model for identifying depressive symptoms in middle-aged and older adults with low haemoglobin. The model may support early screening and risk stratification in this clinically vulnerable population. However, the classification threshold and risk-stratification cut-offs are exploratory rather than clinically validated. Further multicentre validation is warranted before broader clinical implementation.

papers.title: A machine learning model for predicting cognitive improvement after scalp cluster needling therapy in patients with post-stroke mild cognitive impairment.
papers.abstract: Cognitive recovery varies substantially among patients with post-stroke mild cognitive impairment (PSCI-MCI), whereas individualized models for predicting post-treatment cognitive improvement remain limited. This study aimed to develop and internally validate a machine learning model for predicting cognitive improvement after 1 month of scalp cluster needling therapy with prolonged needle retention (SCNT-PR) in patients with PSCI-MCI. This retrospective study included hospitalized patients diagnosed with PSCI-MCI between January 1, 2010, and January 1, 2023. Baseline data included demographics, vascular risk factors, stroke severity, imaging features, cognitive and functional assessments, emotional and sleep-related indicators, treatment-related variables, and laboratory findings. The outcome was defined as an increase of at least 2 points in the corrected Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) score after treatment compared with baseline. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression and the Boruta algorithm were used to identify key predictors. Seven supervised machine learning algorithms were applied to develop pretreatment prediction models. Model performance was assessed in terms of discrimination, calibration, and clinical utility, and Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) were used for model interpretation. A total of 750 patients were included and randomly assigned to a training set (n = 526) and a validation set (n = 224). Seven key predictors were identified from the intersection of LASSO regression and Boruta. Among the evaluated models, LightGBM showed the acceptable performance, with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.759. Calibration curves and decision curve analysis indicated acceptable calibration and favorable clinical utility. SHAP analysis identified baseline corrected MoCA score, years of education, National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale total score, Barthel Index score for activities of daily living, age, frontal lobe lesion, and diabetes as the major contributors to model prediction. Sensitivity analyses demonstrated consistent predictor patterns under alternative outcome definitions and predictor configurations. We developed and internally validated a machine learning model based on multidimensional pretreatment clinical data to predict cognitive improvement after SCNT-PR in patients with PSCI-MCI. This model may provide preliminary support for patient stratification and individualized clinical assessment, although external validation in independent cohorts is required before clinical implementation.
keywords: scalp cluster needling therapy with prolonged needle retention

papers.title: Creative patient and public engagement to amplify the voices of people living with eczema.
papers.abstract: Qualitative research has captured human experiences of suffering associated with atopic eczema. We aimed to convey this information beyond academic manuscripts to a broader audience, using ambitious, multidisciplinary patient and public engagement, led by creative researchers. We worked with patient communities to find ways to amplify eczema voices, using previously reported and newly collected quotes describing their experiences. The resulting "Surface Echoes" project combined audio and visual methods, developed by a collaborative team of creatives, working with stakeholder participants. A script for reading aloud in small groups, and a digital audio recording were created through a process of collaging the collected quotes, curated by the patient communities, creatives and researchers. Themes presented in this work include visual appearance and mental burden of embarrassment or shame (" it's a kind of social handicap…"); pain and itch; lack of clarity around treatment (" I think this 'trial and error' is a very primitive form of medicine"); challenges of communicating with healthcare professionals; and the morbidity associated with sleep deprivation (" It's impossible to be on sick leave just because you are tired. So I carried on throughout the Spring and then I completely collapsed"). The curated quotes also report positive healthcare experiences, indicative of good practice: " I felt listened to … it was a conversation". Project participants used creative research methods to develop imaginaries of better futures, for example, " … sunshine soup" and "… consistent advice". The materials have been used with stakeholders including medical and nursing professionals, industrial and academic researchers, and the public. This work has been designed to raise awareness, promote discussion, reduce stigma and increase understanding of eczema. The presentation to stakeholder groups prioritised by the participants whose voices are amplified was designed to improve empathic discussion with professionals; it may also inform future research.
keywords: art; atopic eczema; creative; multidisciplinary; public-patient participation

papers.title: Device-Measured 24-h Movement Behaviors and Arterial Intima-Media Thickness in Young Adults.
papers.abstract: Physical activity, including light physical activity (LPA) and moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA), sedentary behavior (SED), and sleep, often referred to as "24-h movement behaviors", are modifiable behaviors that may be associated with arterial intima-media thickness (IMT). However, their combined associations with arterial IMT, especially aortic IMT, where cardiometabolic risk burden may be reflected at an earlier age, have not been studied before. This study examined how 24-h movement behaviors associate with aortic and carotid IMT among young adults. Participants (n = 327) were healthy young adults (mean age 26.1 years, SD 0.2) from the Special Turku Coronary Risk Factor Intervention Project (STRIP). 24-h movement behaviors were measured using a wrist-worn accelerometer for 1 week. Aortic and carotid IMT were measured with ultrasonography. Associations between 24-h movement behaviors and aortic and carotid IMT were analyzed using compositional data analysis and compositional isotemporal substitution analysis, adjusting for sex, education, smoking, and distribution of dietary fats. Descriptive model-based estimations indicated lower aortic IMT values for compositions with a higher proportion of LPA. However, theoretical time reallocations between LPA and other behaviors did not indicate significant differences in aortic IMT (e.g., 30 min from sleep to LPA, -0.005 mm [95% CI -0.020-0.010 mm], from SED to LPA, -0.006 mm [95% CI -0.018-0.006], and from MVPA to LPA, -0.008 mm [95% CI -0.038-0.021]). No associations were found for carotid IMT either. No apparent associations were observed between 24-h movement behaviors and arterial IMT among young adults.
papers.journal: Scandinavian journal of medicine & science in sports

papers.title: Should Coffee Consumers Not Have Their Habitual Morning Coffee Before Testing Their Cognitive Functions?
papers.abstract: Caffeine could improve cognitive functions, but study protocols usually prohibit drinking coffee before cognitive testing. However, regular coffee consumers may experience withdrawal effects when they cannot drink their habitual coffee, which may impair cognitive performance. Therefore, we tested the effects of overnight coffee abstinence in regular coffee consumers: once allowing to drink their coffee and once not drinking coffee. The cognitive performance was compared with non-regular coffee consumers. Thirty regular coffee consumers (RCCs) and 25 non-regular consumers (N-RCCs) took part in this study. RCCs were tested after their habitual morning coffee (c-RCC) and after overnight abstinence (a-RCC); N-RCCs were tested once. A cognitive battery assessed reaction time (RT), processing speed (digit symbol substitution test), working memory, verbal learning/memory and executive function (Stroop). Sleep quality was included as a covariate. Compared to c-RCC, overnight coffee abstinence significantly slowed RTs but did not affect the performance in the other cognitive tasks. In the a-RCC condition, but not the c-RCC condition, the RTs were slower than those of the N-RCCs, while accuracy measures were comparable across groups. Sleep quality did not alter these findings. Overnight coffee abstinence selectively slowed RT, and no statistical support was found for effects on memory or executive function. This suggests that overnight coffee abstinence protocols may introduce withdrawal-related RT slowing as a confound in habitual consumers, whereas other cognitive domains may not be affected. Allowing habitual consumers to maintain normal coffee intake could reduce this bias, supporting tailored rather than uniform abstinence requirements based on the specific outcomes studied.

papers.title: Modeling the Selective and Lossy Nature of Visual Processing Bridges the Discrepancy in Noninvasive Neural Decoding.
papers.abstract: Noninvasive neural decoding seeks to infer visual stimuli from brain recordings, such as EEG and MEG, thereby providing a computational approach for probing human visual information processing. Current contrastive learning approaches align brain signals with image embeddings from pretrained neural networks. However, these methods often struggle with the intrinsic visual-brain discrepancy arising from systematic representational gaps and noise because brain signals are treated as direct, lossless replicas of visual inputs. To alleviate this mismatch, the proposed framework accounts for the selective and information-compressive characteristics of biological vision. On the visual side, the framework incorporates an adaptive, context-aware visual calibration mechanism, where multilevel blurred representations are dynamically fused under the guidance of structural salience to refine visual features toward the brain's abstraction level. On the brain-signal side, a robust and lightweight neural encoder is used to mitigate inter-channel and temporal variations. Experiments on standard EEG and MEG benchmarks show that the proposed method achieves strong brain-to-image retrieval performance. Our modeling hypothesis, supported by retrieval behavior, suggests that computational representations aligning with salient and structurally meaningful content better match macroscopic neural responses than fine-grained image details. These findings suggest that incorporating the lossy and selective characteristics of human visual processing into computational models is important for advancing noninvasive neural decoding and understanding brain-machine alignment. The source codes are available at SLVP.

papers.title: Mindfulness-based perioperative care, sleep architecture, autonomic regulation, and early atrial tachyarrhythmia recurrence after radiofrequency catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation: a prospective observational cohort study.
papers.abstract: This study aimed to examine the relationship between perioperative care by mindfulness and sleep quality, autonomic regulation, inflammatory activity, and early recurrence of atrial tachyarrhythmia (AT) following radiofrequency catheter ablation (RFCA) for atrial fibrillation (AF). This was a prospective assessor-blinded observational cohort study involving 124 patients with AF who underwent their initial radiofrequency catheter ablation from April 2023 to December 2025. Conventional perioperative care was provided to one group (n=62), while the other group (n=62) received mindfulness-based perioperative care. To reduce baseline imbalance, propensity score overlap weighting was implemented. Objective sleep architecture was assessed by overnight polysomnography and autonomic function was examined by HRV analysis. hs-CRP, IL-6, TNF-α, IL-1β, and MCP-1 were analyzed by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays. Health related quality of life was determined based on the SF-36 questionnaire. Compared with conventional care, mindfulness-based perioperative care was associated with greater observed changes in total sleep time (389.4 ± 43.8 vs. 365.7 ± 45.2 min, P=0.012), sleep efficiency (77.4 ± 7.2% vs. 71.2 ± 7.8%, P=0.004), sleep onset latency (27.1 ± 8.8 vs. 34.8 ± 10.5 min, P=0.009), and PSQI scores (7.2 ± 2.5 vs. 9.3 ± 2.9, P=0.006). The mindfulness group also showed lower inflammatory biomarker levels and differences in short-term autonomic indices, including a lower LF/HF ratio (1.39 ± 0.41 vs. 1.66 ± 0.54, P=0.005). Early atrial tachyarrhythmia recurrence occurred in 6 patients (9.7%) in the mindfulness-based perioperative care group and in 11 patients (17.7%) in the conventional care group, corresponding to a crude risk ratio of 0.55 (95% CI: 0.22-1.38). Mindfulness-based perioperative care was associated with improved objective and subjective sleep quality, more favorable autonomic and inflammatory biomarker profiles, better postoperative quality of life, and a lower observed rate of early atrial tachyarrhythmia recurrence after radiofrequency catheter ablation for AF.

papers.title: Channel-Adaptive Temporal Modeling with Grouped Convolutional Network and Informer for Seizure Detection and Prediction.
papers.abstract: Reliable identification and early prediction of epileptic seizures play a critical role in improving patient outcomes and supporting timely therapeutic decision-making. To address the challenges of spatiotemporal feature coupling and long-range dependency modeling in multi-channel EEG signals, this paper proposes a channel-adaptive temporal modeling framework named GCNN-Informer. The framework follows a three-stage pipeline: a grouped convolutional network (GCNN) extracts local features and selects the five most discriminative channels; a convolutional block attention module (CBAM) performs dual spatiotemporal enhancement; and a lightweight Informer encoder captures global temporal dependencies via the ProbSparse self-attention mechanism. Experiments on the CHB-MIT dataset, conducted under a patient-specific evaluation scheme, demonstrated that the proposed method achieved accuracies of 97.33% for seizure detection and 97.28% for seizure prediction, with a low false detection rate (FDR) of 0.30/h and a false prediction rate (FPR) of 0.03/h. Grad-CAM visualization further shows that as EEG signals evolve from normal/interictal to preictal and then to ictal stages, the model's attention heatmap progressively transitions from locally sparse highlighting to continuous block-like highlighting, and finally to dense deep-red responses - a pattern that closely aligns with clinical electrophysiological dynamics. This study provides an accurate and generalizable deep-learning solution for real-time epileptic monitoring and early-warning systems.

papers.title: Cofactors in Anaphylaxis: Insights From the European Anaphylaxis Registry.
papers.abstract: The role of cofactors contributing to anaphylaxis severity remains unclear. We analysed data from the European Anaphylaxis Registry (2007-2024) to determine the impact of suspected cofactors on reaction severity. Adjusted odds ratios (aOR) were calculated for the number of organ systems affected, but also two severity classification systems (Ring/Messmer and Brown). At least one suspected cofactor was reported in 8310 cases (49%) out of 16,915. Cofactors were less frequently suspected among younger patients (< 18 years: 26% and ≥ 18 years: 59%). Medication was the most common suspected cofactor in adults (41%), followed by exercise (27%), which was in parallel the most frequent suspected cofactor in children (19%). Emotional burden (children 3%/adults 8%), alcohol (0.4%/8%), sleep deprivation (0.5%/2%) and menstruation (2%/4%) were less commonly reported. We observed a trend between reaction severity and an increasing number of suspected cofactors. Among suspected cofactors, we observed consistent effects on anaphylaxis reaction severity for acute infections among children and alcohol consumption among adults in food-induced reactions. Moreover, we identified an association between the presence of a suspected cofactor(s) and an increased time interval between exposure and onset of symptoms across all age groups in food-induced anaphylaxis. Our data suggest an age-dependent role of suspected cofactors in anaphylaxis severity. Clinicians should explore the presence of cofactors in patients who experienced anaphylaxis, in particular in those with prolonged time intervals between exposure and reaction onset.
